removal_mechanisms.no_confidence: Lower house / legislature passes a vote of no confidence (or government loses confidence/supply)
removal_mechanisms.constructive_no_confidence: Legislature elects a successor and thereby removes the head of government (e.g. FRG Art. 67, Spain 1978, Israel since 2001)
removal_mechanisms.general_election: Loses a scheduled or snap general election
removal_mechanisms.loss_of_party_leadership: Ruling party replaces its leader, who then resigns as head of government
removal_mechanisms.royal_dismissal: Monarch/emperor dismisses the minister or head of government
removal_mechanisms.impeachment: Formal impeachment / removal trial by legislature or court
removal_mechanisms.party_congress: Removed by party Central Committee / Politburo / congress (one-party states)
removal_mechanisms.assassination: Assassination (event, not a procedure; listed where historically common)
removal_mechanisms.death_in_office: Lifetime office; ends only with death (plus other listed mechanisms)
removal_mechanisms.religious_council: Removal by a clerical body (e.g. Iran's Assembly of Experts)
removal_mechanisms.junta_decision: Removed by the ruling junta / military high command (e.g. Argentina 1976-83, Brazil 1964-85)
removal_mechanisms.family_council: Royal family / dynastic council deposes the ruler (e.g. Saudi Arabia 1964)

nations.name: Austria (Habsburg Monarchy / Austria-Hungary / Republic)

periods.name: Habsburg Monarchy (Archduchy of Austria; Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire)
periods.succession: Hereditary Habsburg-Lorraine succession (Pragmatic Sanction). The State Chancellor/foreign minister acts as leading minister.

periods.name: Austrian Empire (Metternich system)
periods.succession: Francis II proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria (Aug 1804) and dissolved the HRE (Aug 1806). Vienna occupied by Napoleon 1805 and 1809.
periods.notes: Under the incapacitated Ferdinand I (1835-48) a State Conference (Archduke Ludwig, Metternich, Kolowrat) ruled.

periods.name: Austrian Empire (revolution and neo-absolutism)
periods.succession: Revolution forces Metternich out (Mar 1848); Ferdinand abdicates for Franz Joseph (2 Dec 1848). Constitutions of 1848/49 revoked by the Sylvester Patent (Dec 1851).

periods.name: Austrian Empire (constitutional experiments)
periods.succession: October Diploma (1860) and February Patent (1861) create an Imperial Council; ministers remain responsible to the emperor. Defeat by Prussia (1866) leads to the Compromise with Hungary.

periods.name: Austria-Hungary (Dual Monarchy)
periods.capital: Vienna (Budapest for the Kingdom of Hungary)
periods.succession: Emperor of Austria is also King of Hungary. Two governments (Cisleithania/Austria and Hungary), each with a Minister-President; three common ('k.u.k.') ministries for Foreign Affairs, War and Finance answer to the monarch. Minister-Presidents served at the emperor's pleasure; Reichsrat obstruction often led to rule by Emergency Decree (§14).
periods.notes: Game: the Austrian Minister-President is head of government; the common Foreign, War and Finance Ministers are the cabinet. Hungarian Minister-Presidents (e.g. Andrássy 1867-71, Kálmán Tisza 1875-90, István Tisza 1903-05, 1913-17) are a separate, powerful actor.

periods.name: Republic of (German-)Austria (First Republic)
periods.succession: Chancellor elected by the National Council (to 1929), then appointed by the President after the 1929 constitutional amendment; responsible to parliament. President elected by the Federal Assembly (direct election introduced 1929 but not held).

periods.name: Federal State of Austria (Austrofascism / Ständestaat)
periods.succession: Dollfuss suspended parliament (Mar 1933); Fatherland Front sole party; civil war Feb 1934; May 1934 corporatist constitution. Dollfuss murdered in the Nazi July Putsch (1934). Ended by German annexation (Anschluss, 13 Mar 1938).

periods.name: Annexed to Germany (Ostmark / Alpine and Danube Reichsgaue)
periods.succession: Part of Nazi Germany; see DEU. Seyss-Inquart Reichsstatthalter 1938-39, then Gauleiters (Bürckel, Schirach).

periods.name: Second Republic under Allied occupation
periods.succession: Renner provisional government (Apr 1945) recognized by the Allies; Allied Council could veto legislation. State Treaty (15 May 1955) restored full sovereignty; permanent neutrality declared Oct 1955.

periods.name: Second Republic (sovereign, neutral; EU member from 1995)
periods.succession: Federal President directly elected (6-year term, max two); appoints and may dismiss the Chancellor and government. National Council can force out the government by a (non-constructive) no-confidence vote - first successful use 27 May 2019 against Kurz. Coalition governments are the norm.
periods.notes: Since 2025: ÖVP-SPÖ-NEOS coalition under Stocker.

role_notes.head_of_government: 1789-1848: no formal prime minister - the State Chancellor / foreign minister (Kaunitz, Thugut, Stadion, Metternich) acted as leading minister. 1852-61 the emperor presided over the government himself (neo-absolutism) with a chairman of the ministers' conference. 1867-1918 the list is the Austrian (Cisleithanian) Minister-President; Hungary had its own Minister-President. 1938-45 no Austrian government (part of Germany).
role_notes.foreign: 1867-1918 the common (k.u.k.) Foreign Minister also chaired the joint Council of Ministers - in game, treat him as the senior advisor. 1920-36 chancellors frequently held foreign affairs themselves; that span is flagged uncertain. No foreign minister 1938-45.
role_notes.defense: Before 1848 military administration lay with the Court War Council (Hofkriegsrat), whose presidents are not listed. Separate Landwehr/Honvéd ministries existed in each half of the Dual Monarchy. No army 1945-55; ministry created 1956. Austria is permanently neutral since 1955 (game should restrict alliances).
role_notes.finance: 1867-1918 the common Finance Minister handled only joint expenditure (and Bosnia); each half also had its own finance minister. 1919-38 coverage partial.
role_notes.interior: Cisleithanian interior ministers 1867-1918 (except Taaffe) and First Republic 1918-38 interior/security ministers not listed - game should fall back to the generic title 'Minister of the Interior'. Security under Austrofascism was run by Vice-Chancellor/Security Minister Emil Fey (1933-35).
role_notes.intelligence: No public civilian intelligence chief before the Second Republic. Staatspolizei (1945-2002) heads not listed. Use the generic title where no holder exists.
role_notes.military_chief: Second Republic chiefs before 2008 not listed; use the generic 'Chief of the General Staff' title.

role_notes.head_of_state: Colonial era: the Portuguese monarch. Regents of the Empire (1831-40) and Princess Isabel (regent during Pedro II's travels 1871-72, 1876-77, 1887-88) are listed as acting. Republic: the President is head of state and of government.
role_notes.head_of_government: 1789-1808: Viceroys of Brazil. 1808-1847: no formal premier - rulers.org lists the Minister of the Kingdom (Reino; from 1822 of the Empire, Império) as principal minister. 1847-1889: President of the Council of Ministers (Presidente do Conselho de Ministros). 1889-1961 and 1963-present: presidential system, the President is head of government. Sep 1961 - Jan 1963: Prime Ministers under the parliamentary Additional Act.
role_notes.foreign: Ministro dos Negócios Estrangeiros (Empire), Ministro das Relações Exteriores (Itamaraty) from 1889. Pre-independence (1808-1821) foreign affairs were handled by Portuguese crown ministers in Rio and are not listed.
role_notes.defense: Minister of War (Ministro da Guerra) 1822-1967; Minister of the Army (Ministro do Exército) Mar 1967 - Jun 1999 (Navy and, from 1941, Air Force had separate ministries); Minister of Defence (Ministro da Defesa, civilian) from 10 Jun 1999. Pre-1822 Portuguese war ministers in Rio are omitted.
role_notes.finance: Ministro da Fazenda (Finance/Treasury) 1822-1990 and 1992-2019 and again from 2023; Ministro da Economia, Fazenda e Planejamento 1990-92 and Ministro da Economia 2019-2022 (super-ministry).
role_notes.interior: Empire: Minister of the Empire (Negócios do Império, the home/interior ministry, 1822-1889). Republic: Minister of Justice and Internal Affairs (Justiça e Negócios Interiores, 1891-1967), then Minister of Justice (Justiça; Justiça e Segurança Pública 2018-19 and from 2023), which controls the Federal Police. The separate 'Ministério do Interior' of 1967-1990 was a regional-development ministry and is not mapped here.
role_notes.intelligence: Serviço Nacional de Informações (SNI) 1964-1990 - its chief had cabinet rank and two chiefs (Médici, Figueiredo) became president. 1990-1999 intelligence was a secretariat of the presidency (SAE) with no prominent public chief; Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (ABIN) from Dec 1999, director-general under the Institutional Security Cabinet (GSI).
role_notes.military_chief: Chief of the Armed Forces General Staff (EMFA, minister-rank, 1946-1999) and Chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces (EMCFA, from 2010). No joint chief existed before 1946 (the Army chief of staff was subordinate to the War Minister) or between 1999 and 2010 (the service commanders reported to the Defence Minister). Game: for those gaps, use the War/Army minister (defense list) as the military chief.

uncertain: Minister lists before Apr 1964 (War, Finance, Empire, Justice, Foreign) and EMFA/EMCFA are transcribed from pt.wikipedia tables (which cite the ministries' official galleries); from Apr 1964 Foreign, War/Army/Defence, Finance and Justice come from rulers.org's Brazilian ministries page. Short interim stand-ins nested inside a minister's term were dropped.
Brief acting stand-ins (<45 days) between two terms of the same minister were folded into that minister's tenure.

2026 changes (Finance: Fernando Haddad -> Dario Durigan, Mar 2026; Justice: Ricardo Lewandowski -> Wellington César Lima e Silva, Jan 2026) agree between rulers.org and pt.wikipedia but were not checked against gov.br.
ABIN director-general dates after 2008 are approximate (prose source); intelligence 1990-1999 (SAE) not listed.
No joint military chief 1889-1946 and 1999-2010 (see role note).

nations.name: Canada

periods.name: Dominion of Canada
periods.succession: Westminster system under the British Crown, represented by a Governor General appointed on the British government's advice. PM is the leader commanding a House of Commons majority.
periods.notes: Foreign policy and declarations of war controlled by London until the 1920s (Canada entered WWI automatically in 1914). The 1926 King-Byng affair shows the Governor General's reserve power to refuse dissolution. Game: Canada cannot conduct independent diplomacy before ~1923 (Halibut Treaty) and becomes fully autonomous with the Statute of Westminster (Dec 1931).

periods.name: Canada (autonomous dominion / Commonwealth realm)
periods.succession: Separate declaration of war in Sep 1939 (one week after the UK). Governor General Canadian-born from 1952. Constitution still amended by the UK Parliament until patriation.
periods.notes: Minority governments common and fragile (1957, 1962-68, 1972-74, 1979).

periods.name: Canada
periods.succession: Constitution Act 1982 patriated the constitution and added the Charter of Rights. Fixed election dates (2007 law) but a minority government may still fall on confidence. Party leaders chosen by membership vote; a new party leader becomes PM without an election (Turner 1984, Campbell 1993, Martin 2003, Carney 2025).
periods.notes: Game: remove a Canadian player via a Commons no-confidence vote (last successful 2011), an election defeat, or a party/caucus revolt forcing resignation (Trudeau 2025). No coups.

role_notes.head_of_state: The monarch is represented in Canada by the Governor General (not listed). The game may show the GG as the in-country head-of-state figure.
role_notes.foreign: No Canadian foreign minister 1867-1909; external relations were conducted by the British Foreign Office (game: London decides for Canada). 1912-1946 the post was held by the PM.
role_notes.interior: Canada has no interior ministry in the European sense. The 1873-1936 'Minister of the Interior' handled western lands and settlement, not security, and is not used. Policing/security: Minister of Justice (RCMP/NWMP, 1867-1966; not listed), Solicitor General (1966-2003), Minister of Public Safety (2003-). Game: for 1867-1965 use the Minister of Justice as a generic advisor.
role_notes.intelligence: No separate public intelligence chief before CSIS (Jul 1984); domestic security intelligence was the RCMP Security Service (1950s-1984). Canada has no foreign HUMINT service; the Communications Security Establishment (SIGINT) chief is not listed.
role_notes.military_chief: 1867-1904 the militia was commanded by a British General Officer Commanding; 1904-1964 the Chief of the General Staff (army), Chief of the Naval Staff and Chief of the Air Staff were coequal (not listed). From 1951 the Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee coordinated them; from Aug 1964 the Chief of the Defence Staff. For the game, 1867-1950 the senior officer is unlisted - use a generic 'Chief of the General Staff'.

uncertain: Current (2026) holders are carried forward from the May 2025 Carney ministry; no 2026 shuffle was found, but this was not exhaustively verified.
Minister of Finance Jun-Sep 1926 (Meighen ministry acting minister) needs verification.
Solicitor General Jan-Jun 1993 (between Doug Lewis and Kim Campbell) needs verification.
CSIS directors 1984-1994 and Chairmen of the Chiefs of Staff Committee 1951-1964: years confirmed, months approximate.
Chief of the General Staff 1904-1964 not covered.

nations.name: China (Qing Empire / Republic of China / People's Republic of China)

periods.name: Great Qing Empire
periods.succession: Hereditary; the emperor secretly designated an heir (from Yongzheng's time). Minor emperors ruled through regents (Cixi). The Grand Council (軍機處) and Six Boards formed the inner government; no prime minister until the 1911 cabinet.
periods.notes: Opium Wars (1839-42, 1856-60), Taiping Rebellion (1850-64), Self-Strengthening, Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), Boxer Uprising (1900), late-Qing constitutional reforms (1906-11). Ended by the Xinhai Revolution. Game: removal of the player = revolution or palace coup (1861 Xinyou, 1898 Wuxu).

periods.name: Republic of China: Beiyang (Beijing) government
periods.succession: Presidents elected by the National Assembly (often coerced or bribed); premiers needed parliamentary approval but changed with warlord fortunes. Real power with Beiyang warlord cliques (Anhui, Zhili, Fengtian) from 1916.
periods.notes: Warlord era; frequent coups. Rival southern (Guangzhou) governments under Sun Yat-sen 1917-25. Game: treat as fragmented; coups common.

periods.name: Republic of China: Nationalist (Kuomintang) Government
periods.succession: KMT 'political tutelage': the party Central Executive Committee appointed the National Government. 1947 Constitution introduced an elected president (by the National Assembly) from 1948.
periods.notes: Japanese invasion 1937-45; Civil War with the CCP 1945-49. Xi'an Incident 1936 (Chiang kidnapped). Japanese puppet regimes (Manchukuo 1932-45, Wang Jingwei 1940-45) not modeled. Government retreated to Taipei 1949-12 (see TWN).

periods.name: People's Republic of China (early Mao era)
periods.succession: CCP Chairman (Mao) supreme; state posts filled by the National People's Congress on party nomination.
periods.notes: Korean War, First Five-Year Plan, Great Leap Forward (1958-62).

periods.name: PRC: Cultural Revolution
periods.succession: Mao's personal authority; designated successors purged (Liu Shaoqi 1968, Lin Biao 1971). State presidency vacant from 1968 and abolished 1975.
periods.notes: Ended with Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four (1976-10, effectively a palace coup).

periods.name: PRC: Reform era (post-Mao)
periods.succession: General Secretary chosen by the Central Committee at party congresses (every 5 years) after Politburo Standing Committee consensus; state president and premier elected by the NPC. Term limits (1982) removed for the presidency in 2018.
periods.notes: Game: the player is the General Secretary; removal = Politburo/Central Committee vote (Hu Yaobang 1987, Zhao Ziyang 1989) or mass unrest. No no-confidence vote.

role_notes.head_of_government: Qing (to 1911): no head of government in the modern sense. The emperor ruled through the Grand Council (軍機處); its leading Grand Councillor is the closest analogue (e.g. Heshen under Qianlong, Prince Gong 1861-84, Prince Li/Shiduo 1884-1898, Ronglu 1898-1903) but the list is not modeled. Powerful regional viceroys such as Li Hongzhang (Zhili, 1870-95, 1900-01) and Zeng Guofan effectively ran diplomacy and military modernization. PRC: Premier of the State Council (government), under the party General Secretary (see paramount_leader).
role_notes.paramount_leader: Use paramount_leader as the player's office for Qing regencies (Cixi), the KMT era (Chiang Kai-shek) and the PRC (CCP Chairman/General Secretary, plus Deng Xiaoping 1978-89 who held no top formal post).
role_notes.foreign: Qing: before 1861 diplomacy was handled by the Board of Rites, the Lifanyuan (Court of Colonial Affairs) and Canton officials; Zongli Yamen 1861-1901, Waiwubu 1901-11. Beiyang foreign ministers changed very frequently; list is partial.
role_notes.defense: Qing Board of War (兵部) presidents and the 1906 Ministry of the Army not modeled. Beiyang Ministers of War not modeled (power lay with warlords). PRC: the Minister of National Defense is largely a diplomatic/administrative post; real command lies with the CCP Central Military Commission Chairman (Mao, Hua, Deng, Jiang, Hu, Xi).
role_notes.finance: Qing Board of Revenue (戶部) presidents and Beiyang finance ministers not modeled (gap).
role_notes.interior: Qing Board of Civil Appointments / 1906 Ministry of Civil Affairs, Beiyang and Nationalist Ministers of the Interior not modeled (gap). PRC: Minister of Public Security used as interior/police chief (the Ministry of Civil Affairs is a minor welfare portfolio).
role_notes.intelligence: Nationalist era: two services, Juntong (military, Dai Li) and Zhongtong (party, CC Clique/Xu Enzeng); only Juntong listed. PRC before 1983: Central Investigation Department (foreign) and Kang Sheng's security apparatus; Minister of State Security from 1983.
role_notes.military_chief: Qing: no general staff until the 1906-1911 reforms; armies commanded by viceroys (Hunan/Huai/Beiyang armies). PRC: Chief of the General Staff (to 2016) / Joint Staff Department (from 2016); real authority is the CMC Chairman and Vice-Chairmen.

uncertain: Beiyang-era premiers and foreign ministers 1916-1928: very frequent turnover, acting tenures; dates marked uncertain and list is not exhaustive.
Qing Zongli Yamen/Waiwubu leadership after 1884 approximate.
PRC finance minister Wu Bo (1979-80) and Public Security ministers 1972-1977 need confirmation.
PLA Joint Staff chief after Liu Zhenli's 2026-01 removal: successor not confirmed.
Nationalist-era defence/finance holders in 1948-49 collapse uncertain.

periods.succession: Hereditary (Salic law, male primogeniture). Ministers serve at the king's pleasure; there is no prime minister by law, though a 'principal minister' (Necker) dominated.
periods.notes: The Estates-General opened 5 May 1789, declared itself the National Assembly 17 Jun 1789; Bastille 14 Jul 1789. The court was forced from Versailles to Paris 5-6 Oct 1789.

Ministries were abolished 20 Apr 1794 and replaced by 12 executive commissions until Nov 1795.

periods.succession: Led by General de Gaulle (Free French leader from 18 Jun 1940; French National Committee from Sep 1941; French Committee of National Liberation, CFLN, from 3 Jun 1943, co-chaired with Giraud until Nov 1943).
periods.notes: Parallel government to Vichy. Game: playable as a government-in-exile; the CFLN could reorganise its leadership (Giraud was eased out Nov 1943 - Apr 1944).

periods.name: Provisional Government of the French Republic (GPRF)
periods.succession: Chairman of the Provisional Government elected by the Constituent Assembly (from Nov 1945); de Gaulle resigned 20 Jan 1946.
periods.notes: Acted as both head of state and head of government.

periods.name: Fourth Republic
periods.succession: President elected for seven years by Parliament. President of the Council invested by the National Assembly; governments fell to censure/confidence votes or coalition break-ups.
periods.notes: Ended by the May 1958 Algiers crisis (military putsch threat) and de Gaulle's investiture (1 Jun 1958).

periods.name: Fifth Republic
periods.succession: President elected by direct universal suffrage (from 1965; seven-year term until 2002, five-year since; at most two consecutive terms since 2008). The President appoints the Prime Minister; the National Assembly can bring down the government by a censure motion (Art. 49: Pompidou 1962, Barnier Dec 2024, Bayrou lost a confidence vote Sep 2025). The President can be removed only by Parliament sitting as the High Court (Art. 68) for breach of duty.
periods.notes: Cohabitation possible when the President's opponents hold the Assembly (1986-88, 1993-95, 1997-2002). Game: president removed by election/term limit/High Court; PM by censure motion or presidential request.

role_notes.head_of_state: Collective or vacant headship: Provisional Executive Council (10 Aug-21 Sep 1792), National Convention (Sep 1792-Oct 1795, presidency rotated fortnightly), Executive Directory (five Directors, Nov 1795-Nov 1799; all 13 Directors listed with overlapping tenures). Free France (1940-44) is a parallel claimant to Vichy. Game: during collective periods let the player be the most powerful member (Committee of Public Safety leader, then Barras) and use coups/purges as removal.
role_notes.head_of_government: No prime minister existed 1792-1815 (Convention, Directory, Consulate, Empire) or 1849-1870 (Louis-Napoléon governed directly; Ministers of State were spokesmen). The Committee of Public Safety entries (Danton, Robespierre) are de facto leaders of a collective body, listed for game use. During the Directory there is no head of government at all: the Directors collectively directed the ministers. Title changes: Président du Conseil des ministres (1815-30, 1947-59), Président du Conseil (1830-49, 1876-1942), Vice-Président du Conseil (1871-76), Chef du Gouvernement (Vichy 1942-44), Premier ministre (since Jan 1959).
role_notes.foreign: Complete 1789-2026 from rulers.org. Ministries were abolished 20 Apr 1794 - 3 Nov 1795 and replaced by a Commission for External Relations (commissioners listed). Free French national commissioners (1941-44) overlap Vichy ministers.
role_notes.defense: Minister of War 1789-1947 (with a coordinating Minister of National Defence above War/Navy/Air in 1932-1940 and 1946-1948, so overlapping holders with different titles are correct), then National Defence / Armed Forces / Defence / Armies. During 1803-1814 a separate Minister of War Administration (Dejean, Lacuée, Daru) handled supply and is not listed. No minister Apr 1794 - Nov 1795 (Commission of Land Armies). Separate navy ministers are listed under navy_minister; air ministers (1928-1947) are not listed.
role_notes.finance: Controllers-General / Director-General of Finances to 1791, then Minister of Public Contributions (1791-94), Finance (from 1795). Napoleon also had a separate Minister of the Public Treasury (Barbé-Marbois 1801-06, Mollien 1806-14/1815) not listed here. Post-1958 portfolio names vary (Economy and Finance, etc.).
role_notes.interior: Complete 1790-2026 (the Ministry of the Interior was created Aug 1790; before that internal administration belonged to the Secretary of State of the King's Household). Gap Apr 1794 - Nov 1795 (executive commission).
role_notes.intelligence: Ministers of General Police (1796-1802, 1804-1818; Fouché, Savary) are the closest public security/intelligence chiefs of the Revolutionary-Napoleonic era, plus Maupas (Minister of Police 1852-53). From 1818 to 1940 there was no publicly named national intelligence chief: military intelligence (Deuxième Bureau of the General Staff) and the Sûreté générale (Interior Ministry) were run by officials not generally public; the game should model this as an interior-ministry/war-ministry function. Free French BCRA (Passy) 1940-44; DGER/SDECE (1945-1982) and DGSE (1982-) directors are public. The domestic service (DST 1944-2008, DCRI 2008-14, DGSI since 2014) is not listed.
role_notes.military_chief: No permanent general staff before 1871: Napoleon was his own commander-in-chief with Berthier as chief of staff; 1815-1870 the Minister of War was the senior military authority. Chief of the General Staff of the Army 1871-1940 (wartime commanders-in-chief Joffre, Nivelle, Pétain, Foch listed); Vichy's Armistice Army chiefs 1940-42 are NOT covered; armed-forces chief (CEMGDN/CEMA) from Nov 1943. 1948-1951 gap: armed-forces chief post effectively vacant/handled by committee.
role_notes.navy_minister: Ministers of the Navy (and Colonies to 1894) 1789-1947 from rulers.org; merged into Armed Forces/National Defence from 1947.

uncertain: Lecornu: resigned 6 Oct 2025 and reappointed 10 Oct 2025; status after that per rulers.org/worldstatesmen at cut-off (2026-10) - verify against gouvernement.fr before shipping.
Nicolas Lerner (DGSE) and Fabien Mandon (CEMA) shown as incumbent per fr.wikipedia at cut-off.
1792-1795 collective executive: the 'de facto' head-of-government entries (Danton, Robespierre) are an interpretation for game purposes, not formal offices.

Some revolutionary-era dates in the rulers.org source were internally inconsistent; two obvious year typos were corrected (Garat Interior 1793, François de Neufchâteau Interior 1798) and flagged in the note field.
Directors François de Neufchâteau and Treilhard: rulers.org dates (May 1799) conflict with standard accounts (May 1798); entries flagged.
1948-1951 armed-forces chief and Vichy-era army chiefs not covered.

nations.name: Germany (Prussia / German Reich / Federal Republic)

periods.name: Kingdom of Prussia (Holy Roman Empire member)
periods.succession: Hereditary Hohenzollern male primogeniture. Ministers (Kabinettsminister) serve at the king's pleasure.
periods.notes: King governs through a cabinet of ministers; foreign affairs led by 'Kabinettsminister' who doubled as leading minister.

periods.name: Kingdom of Prussia (Napoleonic era & wars of liberation)
periods.succession: Hereditary. Stein-Hardenberg reforms create modern ministries (1808) and the office of State Chancellor (1810).
periods.notes: Defeated at Jena-Auerstedt (1806); Treaty of Tilsit (1807) halves Prussia. Napoleon forced Stein's dismissal (1808).

head_of_government: Heinrich Friedrich Karl vom und zum Stein
foreign: August Friedrich Ferdinand von der Goltz

periods.name: Kingdom of Prussia (German Confederation)
periods.succession: Hereditary. Promised constitution not granted until 1848/1850.

periods.name: Kingdom of Prussia (Revolution of 1848)
periods.succession: March ministries appointed under revolutionary pressure; king dissolved the Prussian National Assembly (Dec 1848) and imposed a constitution.

periods.name: Kingdom of Prussia (constitutional monarchy, 1850 constitution)
periods.succession: Ministers responsible to the king, not the Landtag (three-class franchise). The Landtag could refuse budgets (constitutional conflict 1862-66) but could not remove ministers.

periods.name: North German Confederation (Prussian presidency)
periods.succession: King of Prussia holds the Bundespräsidium; Bismarck is Bundeskanzler and Prussian Minister-President.

periods.name: German Empire (Kaiserreich)
periods.succession: King of Prussia is German Emperor (hereditary). Reichskanzler appointed/dismissed by the Kaiser alone; the Reichstag votes budgets and laws but cannot force out the chancellor (until the October 1918 reforms made the chancellor dependent on Reichstag confidence).
periods.notes: Reich ministries were 'Reichsämter' headed by State Secretaries subordinate to the chancellor, not a collegial cabinet. War ministry remained Prussian (plus Bavarian/Saxon/Württemberg ministries).

periods.name: Revolutionary period (Council of People's Deputies)
periods.succession: Kaiser abdicates 9 Nov 1918; power held by the six-member Rat der Volksbeauftragten (SPD/USPD) until the National Assembly convenes.

periods.name: Weimar Republic (parliamentary)
periods.capital: Berlin (National Assembly sat in Weimar Feb-Sep 1919)
periods.succession: Reichspräsident directly elected for 7 years; appoints/dismisses the Reichskanzler, who also needs Reichstag confidence (Art. 54: simple no-confidence vote, non-constructive). Coup attempts: Kapp Putsch (1920), Beer Hall Putsch (1923).
periods.notes: Art. 48 gives the president emergency decree powers; Art. 25 allows dissolution of the Reichstag.

periods.name: Weimar Republic (presidential cabinets)
periods.succession: Brüning, Papen, Schleicher govern by Art. 48 emergency decree with the president's confidence rather than a Reichstag majority; the president's withdrawal of support is the real removal mechanism.

periods.name: Nazi Germany (Third Reich)
periods.succession: Enabling Act (Mar 1933) ends parliamentary control; NSDAP the sole party (Jul 1933). On Hindenburg's death (Aug 1934) Hitler merges presidency and chancellorship as 'Führer und Reichskanzler'. No legal removal mechanism; only coup/assassination (20 July 1944 plot failed) or defeat. Hitler's testament named Dönitz Reichspräsident.
periods.notes: Ministers rarely met as a cabinet after 1938; power lay with Hitler and party/SS offices.

periods.name: Allied occupation
periods.succession: Supreme authority held by the Allied Control Council (US, UK, France, USSR) from 5 Jun 1945; no German national government.

periods.name: Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany)
periods.succession: Bundeskanzler elected by the Bundestag; removable only by a constructive vote of no confidence (Art. 67 GG), used successfully once (Kohl replaced Schmidt, Oct 1982). Bundespräsident elected by the Federal Convention for 5 years (max two terms); impeachable before the Constitutional Court (Art. 61).

periods.name: Federal Republic of Germany (reunified)
periods.capital: Berlin (Bonn remained seat of government until 1999)
periods.succession: As FRG. Chancellors may also call a confidence vote (Art. 68) to trigger early elections (Schröder 2005, Scholz Dec 2024).

role_notes.head_of_state: Prussian kings 1789-1871; from 18 Jan 1871 the King of Prussia is also German Emperor. 1945-49: Allied Control Council (no German head of state). GDR heads of state are in the DDR nation.
role_notes.head_of_government: Before 1848 Prussia had no formal prime minister except Hardenberg as State Chancellor (1810-22); the 'leading minister' list is the de facto chief minister. Prussian Minister-Presidents after 1871 are omitted except where they were also Reich Chancellor (Roon 1873 and Botho zu Eulenburg 1892-94 were separate). 1945-49: no German government.
role_notes.foreign: Prussian foreign ministers to 1871, then State Secretaries of the Auswärtiges Amt (subordinate to the chancellor) until Feb 1919, then Reich Foreign Ministers. No German foreign minister May 1945-Mar 1951.
role_notes.defense: Prussian War Ministers act for the whole Reich 1871-1919 (Bavaria, Saxony and Württemberg kept their own). After Blomberg (Feb 1938) the post was abolished and Hitler commanded through the OKW (Keitel) - in game, treat the OKW chief as the defence advisor 1938-45. No German armed forces/defence ministry 1945-55. Navy: State Secretary of the Reichsmarineamt (Tirpitz 1897-1916) was a separate office.
role_notes.finance: Prussian finance holders before 1825 omitted (split departments). 1871-79 Reich finance was handled by the Prussian finance minister and the Reichskanzleramt; Reich Treasury (Reichsschatzamt) from 1879.
role_notes.interior: Prussian interior ministers to 1878 (Prussia kept its own interior ministry after 1871 - Prussian holders after 1878 are omitted); Reich domestic affairs under the Reichskanzleramt (1867-79) then the Reichsamt des Innern. Nazi era: the interior ministry lost control of the police to Himmler (1936).
role_notes.intelligence: No public intelligence chief before 1913 (Section IIIb of the General Staff existed from 1889). 1933-45: Abwehr (military) and Gestapo/SD/RSHA (party-state security) coexisted - Abwehr chiefs and Gestapo/RSHA chiefs both listed; game may treat RSHA chief as the security advisor. FRG: two parallel lists - BND (foreign intelligence, primary advisor) and BfV (domestic security); both listed with distinguishing titles. 1945-56: Organisation Gehlen under US control.
role_notes.military_chief: Prussian/German Chief of the (Great) General Staff to 1919; Chef der Heeresleitung 1919-35; Commander-in-Chief of the Army 1935-38; OKW chief 1938-45 (Hitler as supreme commander). No German military 1945-55. Generalinspekteur der Bundeswehr from 1957.

nations.name: India

periods.name: British East India Company rule
periods.succession: Governor-General appointed by the Company's Court of Directors under the Board of Control (London). Princely states (Mysore to 1799, Maratha Confederacy to 1818, Sikh Empire to 1849, Mughal emperor at Delhi nominally to 1857) were separate actors.
periods.notes: Not a sovereign playable India; the game could treat the Marathas, Mysore, the Sikh Empire or Hyderabad as tier-3 states. Ended by the 1857 rebellion and the Government of India Act 1858.

periods.succession: Viceroy and Governor-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of the British Cabinet (Secretary of State for India). Viceroy's Executive Council functioned as a cabinet; Indian members from 1909. Interim Government (Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council) from 2 Sep 1946.

periods.name: Republic of India
periods.succession: President elected for 5 years by an electoral college of MPs and state MLAs; President appoints as PM the leader commanding a Lok Sabha majority. PM and Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Vice-President acts if the presidency falls vacant; the senior-most minister is sworn in as interim PM if a PM dies (Nanda 1964, 1966).
periods.notes: Congress Party dominance; wars with China 1962 and Pakistan 1965, 1971.

periods.name: Republic of India (The Emergency)
periods.succession: Indira Gandhi ruled by decree under Art. 352 emergency powers; elections postponed, civil liberties suspended, opposition jailed.
periods.notes: Ended when Gandhi called elections (Mar 1977) and lost to the Janata Party. Game: an incumbent can suspend no-confidence/elections at a legitimacy cost.

periods.name: Republic of India
periods.succession: As 1950-75. No-confidence has actually removed PMs: Morarji Desai resigned ahead of one (1979), V.P. Singh lost a confidence vote (Nov 1990), Deve Gowda (Apr 1997) and Vajpayee (Apr 1999, by one vote) lost confidence votes. Coalition-era governments 1989-2014.
periods.notes: BJP-led NDA since 2014. President Murmu's term runs to Jul 2027; next general election due 2029.

nations.name: Iran (Persia)

periods.name: Qajar-Zand civil war
periods.succession: Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar held the north from Tehran; the Zand dynasty (Jafar Khan d. Jan 1789, Sayyed Morad Khan Jan-May 1789, Lotf Ali Khan May 1789-1794) held Fars. Lotf Ali Khan was captured at Kerman in 1794. Agha Mohammad was formally crowned Shah in March 1796.
periods.notes: Game: start 1789 Iran as Qajar under Agha Mohammad Khan; a Zand rump state can be a tier-3 rival until 1794.

periods.name: Qajar Persia (absolute monarchy)
periods.succession: Hereditary in the Qajar line; the designated crown prince (vali-ahd) traditionally governed Tabriz/Azerbaijan. Grand Viziers served at the Shah's pleasure and were often executed (Qa'em-Maqam 1835, Amir Kabir 1852).
periods.notes: Russo-Persian wars 1804-13 and 1826-28 (Treaties of Gulistan and Turkmenchay); Anglo-Persian War 1856-57; Naser al-Din Shah assassinated 1896. No regular cabinet until the 1850s-70s; foreign ministry from 1821.

periods.notes: 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention split Persia into spheres of influence.

periods.name: Lesser Autocracy (Estebdad-e Saghir)
periods.succession: Mohammad Ali Shah shelled the Majlis (23 Jun 1908) with the Russian-officered Cossack Brigade and ruled by decree until constitutionalist forces took Tehran and deposed him (16 Jul 1909).

periods.name: Qajar constitutional monarchy (Ahmad Shah)
periods.succession: Ahmad Shah succeeded as a boy under regents (Azod al-Molk 1909-10, Naser ol-Molk 1910-14). Cabinets fell every few months. 1911 Russian ultimatum closed the Second Majlis; WWI occupation by Russian, British and Ottoman forces despite neutrality; 21 Feb 1921 coup by Reza Khan and Zia'eddin Tabatabaee. Majlis deposed the dynasty on 31 Oct 1925.
periods.notes: Ahmad Shah largely absent in Europe after 1923.

periods.name: Pahlavi Iran under Reza Shah
periods.succession: Constituent Assembly made Reza Khan Shah (12 Dec 1925); hereditary in the Pahlavi line. Majlis was a rubber stamp; ministers dismissed (and some, like Teymourtash 1933, killed) at the Shah's will. Country renamed Iran internationally in 1935.
periods.notes: Anglo-Soviet invasion (25 Aug 1941) forced Reza Shah's abdication in favour of his son (16 Sep 1941).

periods.name: Mohammad Reza Shah - parliamentary interlude
periods.succession: Majlis vote of inclination (tamayol) nominated PMs, the Shah issued the farman. Allied occupation to 1946 (Azerbaijan crisis). PMs Hazhir (1949) and Razmara (1951) assassinated. Mosaddegh nationalised oil (1951); the 30 Tir uprising (Jul 1952) restored him after the Shah replaced him with Qavam.
periods.notes: Ended by the Anglo-American-backed coup of 19 Aug 1953 (28 Mordad) that installed Gen. Fazlollah Zahedi.

periods.name: Pahlavi royal autocracy
periods.succession: Shah appointed and dismissed PMs; Majlis managed through official parties (Iran Novin, then the single Rastakhiz Party from 1975). SAVAK from 1957. White Revolution 1963.
periods.notes: Revolution of 1978-79: Shah left Iran 16 Jan 1979 leaving a Regency Council and PM Bakhtiar; the army declared neutrality 11 Feb 1979.

periods.name: Provisional revolutionary government
periods.succession: Khomeini as Leader of the Revolution appointed Bazargan's Provisional Government (named 4-5 Feb 1979) alongside the clerical Council of the Islamic Revolution. Bazargan resigned after the US embassy seizure (6 Nov 1979); the Revolutionary Council governed until 1980.
periods.notes: Islamic Republic proclaimed 1 Apr 1979 after referendum; constitution ratified Dec 1979.

periods.name: Islamic Republic (with prime minister)
periods.succession: Supreme Leader (Vali-ye Faqih) holds ultimate authority; directly elected president plus a PM confirmed by the Majlis. Majlis declared President Banisadr politically incompetent (21 Jun 1981) and Khomeini dismissed him. President Rajai and PM Bahonar killed by a bomb (30 Aug 1981).
periods.notes: Iran-Iraq War 1980-88. 1989 constitutional revision abolished the PM post.

periods.name: Islamic Republic (presidential executive)
periods.succession: Assembly of Experts elects and may in theory dismiss the Supreme Leader (lifetime office). President directly elected (two consecutive 4-year terms) after Guardian Council vetting; Majlis can impeach ministers (used often: Nouri 1998, Kordan 2008, Karbasian 2018, Hemmati 2025) and declare the president incompetent, with the Leader's approval to dismiss. If the president dies, the first vice-president acts and an election follows within 50 days (2024).
periods.notes: Ali Khamenei killed in a US-Israeli strike 28 Feb 2026; an interim Leadership Council (President, Chief Justice, a Guardian Council faqih) served 1-9 Mar 2026 until the Assembly of Experts chose Mojtaba Khamenei. Game: Supreme Leader is the player's office; IRGC loyalty is the key coup/revolution variable.

role_notes.head_of_state: Qajar/Pahlavi Shah, then the Supreme Leader (Vali-ye Faqih), who commands the armed forces, appoints the judiciary chief, half the Guardian Council and the heads of state media, and can dismiss the president. Game: in 1979+ the player is the Supreme Leader; the president is a powerful advisor/rival.
role_notes.head_of_government: Pre-1906: Grand Viziers (Sadr-e A'zam) — there was no cabinet as such; long vacancies (1858-71) when the Shah ruled through a council. 1906-1989: Prime Minister. 1980-89 the President coexisted with the PM (listed here with notes; game should treat the PM as head of government in that window). From Aug 1989 the President is head of government.
role_notes.foreign: Foreign ministry founded 1821; Qajar-era holders are year-only and partly unverified. Pahlavi 1925-38 is not reliably covered (see uncertainty).
role_notes.defense: Before 1858 there was no Minister of War: the Shah, crown prince (Abbas Mirza, 1799-1833) or a royal prince commanded. 1982-1989 a separate Ministry of the IRGC existed (Mohsen Rafiqdoost 1982-88, Ali Shamkhani 1988-89) — not listed as main holders. Since 1989 the MODAFL minister is a procurement/logistics role; operational command runs Supreme Leader -> General Staff.
role_notes.finance: Pre-1906: finances run by the Mostowfi al-Mamalek (chief accountant) and the Shah's treasury; foreign advisers (Shuster 1911, Millspaugh 1922-27, 1943-45) held real fiscal power. Pahlavi-era finance holders 1924-1979 are year-only in available sources and flagged uncertain.
role_notes.interior: Qajar interior ministers (post-1906) are not covered; Pahlavi and Islamic Republic lists complete per Wikipedia cross-check. 1979-80 gap covered by acting ministers (Rafsanjani, others).
role_notes.intelligence: No modern intelligence chief before SAVAK (1957); 1979-84 intelligence was split among IRGC intelligence, revolutionary committees and the PM's office; Ministry of Intelligence (VAJA/MOIS) from 1984. IRGC Intelligence Organization is a parallel, often more powerful service. After Khatib's death (Mar 2026) the ministry was run by an acting minister whose name was not confirmed in sources checked.
role_notes.military_chief: IRGC commanders-in-chief (separate force, politically decisive): Javad Mansouri 1979, Abbas Agha-Zamani 1979-80, Morteza Rezaee 1980-81, Mohsen Rezaee 1981-97, Yahya Rahim Safavi 1997-2007, Mohammad Ali Jafari 2007-19, Hossein Salami 2019-Jun 2025 (killed), Mohammad Pakpour Jun 2025-Feb 2026 (killed), Ahmad Vahidi Mar 2026- (confirmed 10 Aug 2026). Artesh commanders-in-chief since 1998: Ali Shahbazi, Mohammad Salimi, Ataollah Salehi, Abdolrahim Mousavi (2017-25), Amir Hatami (Jun 2025-). Qajar era had no general staff; Persian Cossack Brigade (Russian-officered, 1879-1921) was the main modern unit.

uncertain: Lotf Ali Khan Zand vs Agha Mohammad Khan in 1789-94: two rival rulers; the game should pick Qajar.
Qajar Grand Viziers 1819-1835 and 1858-1886 have year-only or approximate dates; 1873-80 sharing of power between Sepahsalar, Mostowfi al-Mamalek and Kamran Mirza is simplified.
Foreign Ministers: Qajar-era list year-only; Pahlavi 1925-1938 single-holder entry (Nosrat al-Dowleh) conflicts with other sources and is likely wrong.
Finance ministers 1924-1979: year-only from a Wikipedia list flagged for citations.
Interior minister 1979-80 (Revolutionary Council) dates approximate.

2026 war changes: Chief of General Staff vacant/acting Mar-Aug 2026 (holder unknown); acting Intelligence Minister after 18 Mar 2026 unnamed; Defence Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi from 18 Oct 2026 per Wikipedia only; Supreme Leader vote count disputed.
Iran-Israel/US 2026 war ceasefire date not established in sources checked.

nations.name: Israel

periods.name: Provisional Government of Israel
periods.succession: Provisional State Council (Moetzet HaMedina HaZmanit) and Provisional Government governed until the first Knesset convened (14 Feb 1949).
periods.notes: War of Independence 1948-49. Weizmann was President of the Provisional State Council.

periods.name: State of Israel (parliamentary)
periods.capital: Jerusalem (declared capital Jan 1950; Knesset moved Dec 1949). Most foreign embassies stayed in Tel Aviv.
periods.succession: President (elected by the Knesset) asks the MK most likely to form a coalition; government needs Knesset confidence. PM resignation brings down the whole government. Coalition collapse typically leads to Knesset self-dissolution and early elections.
periods.notes: Unicameral 120-seat Knesset, pure national-list proportional representation; every government has been a coalition.

periods.name: State of Israel (directly elected PM)
periods.succession: PM directly elected (1996, 1999, special PM-only election Feb 2001). A Knesset no-confidence vote (61 MKs) removed the PM but forced new elections for both PM and Knesset.
periods.notes: Direct election repealed in 2001 (Basic Law: The Government 2001).

periods.name: State of Israel (parliamentary, constructive no-confidence)
periods.succession: Constructive no-confidence: the Knesset must approve an alternative government (since 2014 amendment) to topple the incumbent. Failure to pass a budget triggers automatic dissolution and elections. Rotation agreements (2020 Netanyahu-Gantz, 2021 Bennett-Lapid) can hand office over without a vote; 'alternate prime minister' post created 2020.
periods.notes: Election for the 26th Knesset scheduled for 27 Oct 2026 (Knesset dissolved July 2026); Netanyahu heads the 37th government at the data cut-off.

role_notes.head_of_state: Ceremonial President elected by the Knesset (7-year single term since 2000; previously 5-year renewable). Pardon power and the mandate to form a government are its main game levers.
role_notes.head_of_government: Real executive. 'Alternate Prime Minister' (2020-) is a designated successor under rotation deals: Gantz 2020-21, Lapid 2021-22, Bennett 2022.
role_notes.intelligence: Three agencies: Mossad (foreign intelligence, listed here), Shin Bet/Shabak (internal security; directors: Isser Harel 1948-52, Izi Dorot 1952-53, Amos Manor 1953-63, Yosef Harmelin 1964-74, Avraham Ahituv 1974-80, Avraham Shalom 1981-86, Yosef Harmelin 1986-88, Yaakov Peri 1988-95, Carmi Gillon 1995-96, Ami Ayalon 1996-2000, Avi Dichter 2000-05, Yuval Diskin 2005-11, Yoram Cohen 2011-16, Nadav Argaman 2016-21, Ronen Bar Oct 2021-Jun 2025 (dismissal contested in court; resigned), acting deputy 'Sh.' Jun-Oct 2025, David Zini Oct 2025-), and Aman (military intelligence directorate). Mossad and Shin Bet report directly to the PM. Mossad directors' exact month boundaries 1949-1968 are approximate.
role_notes.defense: PM frequently holds Defence concurrently (Ben-Gurion, Eshkol, Begin, Rabin, Peres, Barak, Netanyahu).
role_notes.military_chief: Ramatkal is the only lieutenant-general; appointed by the cabinet on the defence minister's recommendation, normally 3-4 year terms.

uncertain: Interior ministry after Oct 2025: reported vacant/held by the PM pending a new appointment; not confirmed as of 2026-10.
27 Oct 2026 Knesset election is after the data cut-off; Netanyahu remains PM (37th government) at cut-off.
Shin Bet acting chief Jun-Oct 2025 is identified publicly only by initial; David Zini start month (Oct 2025) from press reports.

nations.name: Italy

periods.name: Pre-unification (no Italian state)
periods.succession: No unified Italy. The peninsula was divided (Kingdom of Sardinia, Papal States, Two Sicilies, Austrian Lombardy-Venetia, Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy 1805-1814 under Napoleon with Eugène de Beauharnais as viceroy).
periods.notes: Game: Italy should not be playable before 17 Mar 1861; the Kingdom of Sardinia (capital Turin; Cavour PM 1852-1859, 1860-61) is its predecessor if the game models it.

periods.name: Kingdom of Italy (liberal monarchy)
periods.succession: Hereditary Savoy monarchy (Salic law). The Statuto Albertino (1848) made ministers formally responsible to the King, but by convention governments needed the confidence of the Chamber of Deputies; cabinets usually fell to parliamentary crises rather than formal votes. King Umberto I assassinated 1900.
periods.notes: Senate appointed by the King; Chamber elected on a narrow franchise until 1912 (near-universal male suffrage 1912/1918).

periods.name: Fascist Italy
periods.succession: Mussolini appointed after the March on Rome; from 1925-26 'Capo del Governo' answerable only to the King; single-party state from 1926/1928. The Grand Council of Fascism could advise on succession. Removed 25 Jul 1943 when the Grand Council passed the Grandi motion and Victor Emmanuel III dismissed and arrested him.
periods.notes: Game: no-confidence impossible; removal only by royal dismissal backed by a Grand Council revolt (palace coup).

periods.name: Badoglio/Bonomi royal governments; co-belligerent Kingdom of the South
periods.capital: Rome; Brindisi (Sep 1943-Feb 1944); Salerno (Feb-Jul 1944); Rome from Jul 1944
periods.succession: Royal government without an elected parliament; from Jun 1944 cabinets formed by the CLN parties under Allied supervision; Umberto Lieutenant General of the Realm from 5 Jun 1944.
periods.notes: Parallel German puppet state, the Italian Social Republic (RSI, 23 Sep 1943-25 Apr 1945), seat at Salò/Gargnano on Lake Garda: Mussolini head of state and government and his own foreign minister; Rodolfo Graziani minister of defence; Domenico Pellegrini Giampietro finance; Guido Buffarini Guidi then Paolo Zerbino interior. Mussolini executed by partisans 28 Apr 1945.

periods.name: Italian Republic
periods.succession: President elected for 7 years by Parliament in joint session plus regional delegates. Government needs the confidence of BOTH chambers (Art. 94); a government that loses confidence (or whose coalition breaks) resigns and the President consults to form a new one or dissolves Parliament. President removable only for high treason/attack on the Constitution (impeachment by Parliament, trial by Constitutional Court).
periods.notes: Constitution in force 1 Jan 1948. Extremely frequent cabinet changes (68 governments 1946-2022). Monarchy abolished by the 2 Jun 1946 referendum.

role_notes.head_of_government: Before 1926 the PM was formally President of the Council of Ministers; Mussolini held the distinct office of Capo del Governo 1926-1943. PMs frequently held the Interior and/or Foreign portfolio concurrently.
role_notes.defense: 1861-1947: Minister of War (army only; separate Ministers of the Navy and, from 1925, of the Air Force - not listed). Ministry of Defence from 4 Feb 1947.
role_notes.finance: Kingdom: Minister of Finance (Finanze) listed; a separate Treasury (Tesoro) existed 1877-1922 and 1944-1946. Republic 1946-2001: Minister of the Treasury (the senior economic post; a separate Finance ministry handled taxation). From 2001: Minister of Economy and Finance.
role_notes.intelligence: No national intelligence chief before 1925 (army 'Ufficio Informazioni'). 1925-1945 SIM (military); the Fascist political police OVRA was run by the Chief of Police (Bocchini, Senise). 1949-1977 SIFAR then SID (military). 1977-2007 SISMI (military/foreign) and SISDE (civil/domestic, not listed). From 2007 AISE (external) and AISI (internal, not listed). SID/SISMI months are approximate.
role_notes.military_chief: 1882-1925: Chief of Staff of the Army (no joint chief before). 1925-1945: Chief of the General Staff (Capo di Stato Maggiore Generale, Comando Supremo from 1941). Republic: Chief of the Defence Staff (formally so-titled from 1948/1950). The King was nominal commander-in-chief; in 1940 Mussolini took operational command as First Marshal of the Empire.

uncertain: Ministerial start/end dates are taken from the decree dates as given in Italian ministerial lists; a few short ad-interim spells (e.g. Fanfani/Moro in Foreign Affairs 1965-66) are merged.
SID and SISMI directors 1966-2001: month or only year known; flagged.
Carmine Senise's tenure as police chief (1940-43, briefly again Jul-Sep 1943) simplified.

nations.name: Japan

periods.name: Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo bakufu)
periods.capital: Edo (shogun's seat; Emperor resided in Kyoto)
periods.succession: Hereditary shogunate within the Tokugawa house, chosen from the main line or the Gosanke/Gosankyō branch houses; the Emperor is a sacral figure without executive power. Senior councillors (rōjū) run day-to-day government and are dismissed by the shogun.
periods.notes: Feudal military government (bakufu) under a nominal Emperor; seclusion policy (sakoku) until 1854. Ended by the Boshin War/Meiji Restoration. Game: treat shogun as the ruler; 'removal' = palace intrigue (rōjū dismissal) or revolution.

periods.name: Meiji Restoration: Daijōkan (Council of State) government
periods.succession: Imperial rule in name; policy made by an oligarchy of Satsuma-Chōshū leaders (genrō-to-be). Ministers (kyō) appointed by the throne.
periods.notes: Satsuma Rebellion 1877; ministers held -kyō titles until the cabinet system of 1885-12.

periods.name: Empire of Japan: Meiji constitutional order (oligarchic/genrō cabinets)
periods.succession: PM nominated to the Emperor by the genrō (elder statesmen, e.g. Itō, Yamagata, Matsukata, later Saionji). Meiji Constitution 1889 (Diet from 1890-11): cabinet responsible to the Emperor, not the Diet, but needed Diet consent for budgets. Army/Navy ministers had to be serving officers (1900-1913, again 1936-45), giving the services a veto over cabinets.
periods.notes: Game: no formal no-confidence; a hostile Diet can block budgets, and military resignation can topple cabinets ('cabinet collapse' event).

periods.name: Empire of Japan: 'Taishō democracy' party cabinets
periods.succession: Convention ('normal course of constitutional government') that the leader of the majority party in the House of Representatives is nominated by the last genrō Saionji. Universal male suffrage 1925.
periods.notes: PMs Hara (1921) and Hamaguchi (shot 1930) assassinated; ended by the May 15 Incident 1932.

periods.name: Empire of Japan: militarist 'national unity' cabinets
periods.succession: PM chosen by the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal and senior statesmen (jūshin), effectively requiring Army acceptance. Political parties dissolved into the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (1940).
periods.notes: February 26 Incident 1936 (failed army coup). Imperial General Headquarters from 1937. Game: Army can veto/topple cabinets by withholding a War Minister.

periods.name: Allied (U.S.) Occupation
periods.succession: Japanese cabinet governed under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (MacArthur, then Ridgway). New Constitution in force 1947-05-03: PM elected by the Diet.
periods.notes: Military and Home Ministry abolished; Article 9 renounces war. Sovereignty restored by the San Francisco Treaty (in force 1952-04-28).

periods.name: Japan (post-war constitutional monarchy)
periods.succession: PM designated by the National Diet (House of Representatives prevails). A no-confidence resolution forces resignation or dissolution within 10 days. In practice the LDP presidential election chooses the PM (LDP in power 1955-93, 1994-2009, 2012-present).
periods.notes: Emperor is 'symbol of the State'. Self-Defense Forces from 1954. Game: removal mainly by losing the LDP leadership or an election; no-confidence has succeeded in 1948, 1953, 1980, 1993.

role_notes.head_of_state: The Emperor reigned but before 1868 had no executive power; 1868-1945 sovereign in law but acted on advice; since 1947 purely symbolic.
role_notes.paramount_leader: 1789-1868 only: the Tokugawa shogun was the de facto ruler; the game should make the shogun the player's office for this era.
role_notes.head_of_government: 1789-1868: rōjū shuseki / tairō act as chief minister (list here is partial: only major figures). 1871-1885 Daijō-daijin (Sanjō) was nominal; real power with Ōkubo then Itō. Cabinet PM from 1885-12-22.
role_notes.foreign: Before 1869 foreign affairs were handled by bakufu Gaikoku-bugyō (commissioners); not modeled. PMs frequently held the portfolio concurrently for days/weeks; only notable acting stints listed.
role_notes.defense: Pre-1945 the Army Minister is listed as defence and the Navy Minister separately (navy_minister). 1945-1952 no military ministry (Article 9). Defense Agency Director-Generals 1954-2007 (about 60 holders) are only partially listed here — known gap. Minister of Defense from 2007-01-09.
role_notes.interior: Home Ministry abolished 1947-12. 1948-2001 functions split among Ministry of Home Affairs (Jichishō), National Public Safety Commission and others; those ministers are a known gap. Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications from 2001-01.
role_notes.intelligence: No unified intelligence chief before 1945: Army Kempeitai (military police, also political policing in occupied areas) and the Home Ministry Special Higher Police (Tokkō) were the security apparatus; commanders not modeled. Post-war: Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office (Naichō); Director of Cabinet Intelligence from 2001. Only Kitamura Shigeru listed (gap). Public Security Intelligence Agency (PSIA, Ministry of Justice) is a secondary option.
role_notes.military_chief: Pre-1945: Chief of the Army General Staff (the Navy General Staff had its own chief, not listed). Supreme command was independent of the cabinet (tōsuiken). Post-war: Chairman of the Joint Staff Council 1954-2006 (gap), Chief of Staff, Joint Staff from 2006-03.

uncertain: Rōjū shuseki list 1789-1868 is selective; tenures of Mizuno, Abe and Hotta are approximate (lunar-calendar conversions).
Pre-1885 -kyō ministers: Soejima, Ōkubo (finance) and early army minister dates approximate.
Interior (MIC) holders 2022-2024 (Matsumoto/Suzuki sequence) need verification.
MIC minister Fujii Hisayuki (2026-09) from a single Nippon.com summary.
Defense Agency Director-Generals 1954-2007, Joint Staff Council chairmen 1954-2006, Home Affairs ministers 1948-2001: not listed (gap).

periods.succession: Viceroys appointed and recalled by the Spanish Crown (Charles IV to 1808, then Ferdinand VII; Cortes of Cádiz/Regency 1808-14).
periods.notes: Not a sovereign actor before independence. War of Independence 16 Sep 1810 (Grito de Dolores) - 27 Sep 1821. Foreign/defence policy run from Madrid.

periods.succession: Santa Anna recalled by conservatives as dictator; made dictatorship perpetual Dec 1853.
periods.notes: Gadsden Purchase 1853/54. Overthrown by the Revolution of Ayutla (1854-55).

periods.name: Liberal Reform (Ayutla governments; Constitution of 1857)
periods.succession: 1857 Constitution: president elected indirectly for 4 years; the President of the Supreme Court is constitutional successor.
periods.notes: Comonfort's self-coup (Plan of Tacubaya, Dec 1857) triggered the Reform War.

periods.name: Reform War (rival Liberal and Conservative governments)
periods.succession: Liberals recognised Supreme Court president Benito Juárez as constitutional president; Conservatives installed Zuloaga then Miramón in Mexico City.
periods.notes: Game: model as civil war with two claimant governments. The U.S. recognised Juárez in 1859.

periods.name: Restored Constitutional Government (Juárez) and French Intervention
periods.succession: Juárez elected 1861.
periods.notes: Debt moratorium (Jul 1861) led to British-Spanish-French intervention (Dec 1861); French victory at Puebla 1863 and occupation of Mexico City (Jun 1863).

head_of_state: Supreme Provisional Executive Power (Juan Nepomuceno Almonte; Juan Bautista de Ormaechea; Pelagio Antonio de Labastida; José Mariano de Salas)
finance: Manuel María de Zamacona y Murphy

periods.name: Second Mexican Empire (Maximilian I) vs. itinerant Republic
periods.capital: Mexico City (Empire) / San Luis Potosí, Chihuahua, Paso del Norte (Republic)
periods.succession: Assembly of Notables offered the crown to Maximilian of Habsburg (accepted 10 Apr 1864, Miramar). Republican government under Juárez continued (term extended by decree 1865).
periods.notes: French-backed monarchy ruled by imperial decree (Provisional Statute 1865, no constitution). French troops withdrew 1866-67; Maximilian captured at Querétaro and executed 19 Jun 1867.

head_of_state: Supreme Provisional Executive Power (Juan Nepomuceno Almonte; Juan Bautista de Ormaechea; Pelagio Antonio de Labastida; José Mariano de Salas)

periods.name: Restored Republic
periods.succession: 1857 Constitution; Juárez re-elected 1867 and 1871 (died 1872); Lerdo succeeded as Supreme Court president.
periods.notes: Ended by Díaz's Plan of Tuxtepec revolt (1876).

interior: Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada y Corral
Juan José del Refugio Baz Palafox

periods.name: Porfiriato
periods.succession: Nominal elections every 4 (from 1904: 6) years; Díaz re-elected 1884-1910 after amending the no-re-election clause. Vice-presidency restored 1904 (Ramón Corral).
periods.notes: Stable authoritarian modernisation; cabinet of 'científicos'. Revolution began 20 Nov 1910 (Plan of San Luis); Díaz resigned 25 May 1911 (Treaty of Ciudad Juárez).

interior: Juan José del Refugio Baz Palafox
José Trinidad García de la Cadena Varela

periods.name: Maderista Republic
periods.succession: Interim León de la Barra; Madero elected Oct 1911.
periods.notes: Ended by the Decena Trágica coup (9-19 Feb 1913); Madero and VP Pino Suárez murdered 22 Feb 1913.

periods.name: Huerta dictatorship
periods.succession: Huerta became president via Foreign Secretary Lascuráin's 45-minute presidency (constitutional line of succession manipulated).
periods.notes: Constitutionalist revolt (Carranza, Villa, Zapata, Obregón); U.S. occupation of Veracruz Apr-Nov 1914. Huerta resigned 15 Jul 1914.

periods.name: Revolutionary civil war (Constitutionalists vs. Conventionists)
periods.capital: Mexico City (contested; Carranza at Veracruz Nov 1914 - Oct 1915)
periods.succession: Carranza as First Chief of the Constitutionalist Army held executive power; the Convention of Aguascalientes named rival presidents (Gutiérrez, González Garza, Lagos Cházaro).
periods.notes: Game: two claimant governments until Carranza's de facto recognition by the U.S. (Oct 1915). Constitution of 1917 promulgated 5 Feb 1917.

periods.name: Post-revolutionary republic (Sonoran dynasty / early Maximato)
periods.succession: 1917 Constitution: direct election, 4-year term (6 years from 1928), no re-election (briefly relaxed 1927-28 for Obregón).
periods.notes: Carranza killed 1920 after Agua Prieta revolt; Obregón assassinated as president-elect July 1928; Calles as 'Jefe Máximo' dominated 1928-1935 (Maximato). Cristero War 1926-29.

periods.name: PNR/PRM/PRI hegemonic-party era
periods.succession: Single six-year term (sexenio) without re-election; the outgoing president personally chose the PRI candidate ('el dedazo'), who then won non-competitive elections. Interim/substitute presidents are chosen by Congress (Art. 84-85).
periods.notes: Formally a presidential republic with elections, but in practice a dominant-party regime until the 1990s reforms (IFE 1990/1996); PRI lost the lower house in 1997. Game: no coups after 1929 (last major military revolt: Escobar 1929, Cedillo 1938); presidential removal effectively impossible, power ends at the sexenio.

foreign: Jorge Castañeda y Álvarez de la Rosa

periods.name: Multi-party democracy
periods.succession: Direct election, single 6-year term, no re-election ever. Vacancy filled by Congress (Secretary of the Interior acts provisionally since 2012 reform). Since 2019 a presidential recall referendum (revocación de mandato) can remove the president (first held 2022, not binding for lack of turnout).
periods.notes: Impeachment (juicio político) of a sitting president is limited to treason and serious common crimes (Art. 108); since 2021 the president can be tried for corruption. Game: treat recall referendum as a 'no_confidence'-like popular trigger mid-term.

role_notes.head_of_state: 1789-1821 the head of state is the King of Spain (Charles IV 1788-1808, Ferdinand VII 1808-1833 with the Joseph Bonaparte/Regency interlude); viceroys are listed under head_of_government as the local executive. From 1824 the President is both head of state and head of government; 'interim', 'substitute' and 'provisional' presidents are distinct constitutional categories and are marked acting=True with the category in the note.
role_notes.head_of_government: Presidential system: the President of Mexico is head of government (see head_of_state). Only the colonial viceroys (1789-1821) and the Second Empire's Presidents of the Council of Ministers (1864-67) are listed here.
role_notes.foreign: 1821-1843 the ministry was 'Relaciones Exteriores e Interiores' (foreign + interior combined), so the same person appears under interior for those years. From 1858-67 rulers.org lists the Liberal (Juárez) government's ministers by default; Conservative/Imperial ministers are flagged in the note. 19th-century tenures are to the year only (rulers.org); exact dates in the SRE official list where noted.
role_notes.defense: Secretaría de Guerra y Marina 1821-1937; Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional (SEDENA) from 1 Jan 1937. The navy became a separate ministry (Marina Nacional, SEMAR) on 31 Dec 1940 - see navy_minister. SEDENA secretaries are always serving army generals and are the senior officer of the Army and Air Force.
role_notes.military_chief: Mexico has no joint chief of staff: the Secretary of National Defence (an active-duty general) commands the Army and Air Force and the Secretary of the Navy (an active-duty admiral) commands the Navy. Game: map the military chief advisor to the SEDENA secretary (defense list). Pre-1876 armies were led by whichever caudillo held the presidency or field command.
role_notes.intelligence: Public chiefs only: Dirección Federal de Seguridad (DFS, 1947-1985, political police under Gobernación); DISEN (1985-89); CISEN (1989-2018); Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI, Dec 2018-). Before 1947 no national intelligence chief existed (intelligence was a Gobernación/army function).
role_notes.interior: 1821-1843 the interior portfolio was combined with foreign affairs ('Relaciones Exteriores e Interiores'), then 'Relaciones Exteriores, Gobernación y Policía' 1842-53; Gobernación separate from 1853. Since 2012 reform the Secretary of the Interior (Gobernación) is first in the line of provisional presidential succession. Public security was split off to SSP (2000-2013) and SSPC (2018-).
role_notes.finance: Secretaría de Hacienda (y Crédito Público from 1891). Officials marked acting were 'encargados del despacho' (oficial mayor / undersecretary in charge).

uncertain: 19th-century foreign ministers (1821-1919) are dated to the year only (rulers.org); exact day-level dates exist in the SRE's official list but were not transcribed.

Defence, Navy, Finance and Interior holders come from the INAP cabinet compendium (Quijano Torres 2012) as tabulated on Spanish Wikipedia; brief acting stand-ins (<45 days) that interrupt the same minister were folded into the minister's tenure.

Reform War (1858-61) and Second Empire (1863-67): two rival governments existed; holders of the Conservative/Imperial side are flagged in notes. Defence/finance/interior lists may mix both sides for those years.
DISEN period (Aug 1985 - Feb 1989) intelligence directors not listed (not reliably public).
2026 change of Foreign Secretary (Juan Ramón de la Fuente -> Roberto Velasco Álvarez) taken from rulers.org/es.wikipedia; not verified against an official SRE announcement.

nations.name: Ottoman Empire / Turkey

periods.name: Ottoman Empire (classical/early reform era)
periods.succession: Sultan chosen from the House of Osman (seniority/agnatic, not primogeniture); deposition by Janissary revolt or palace coup was common (Selim III 1807, Mustafa IV 1808). Grand Viziers served at the Sultan's pleasure and were dismissed, exiled or executed at will.
periods.notes: No cabinet: the Imperial Council (Divan-ı Hümayun) under the Grand Vizier; foreign affairs handled by the Reis ül-Küttab (chief scribe) until the Foreign Ministry was created in 1836; the Janissary Agha and later the Serasker (1826) led the army.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire (Tanzimat)
periods.succession: As above. The Sultan remained absolute but a Council of Ministers (Meclis-i Vükelâ) with Western-style ministries (Foreign 1836, Interior 1836/37, Finance 1838) emerged; the Grand Vizier led it. Abdülaziz was deposed by his ministers in 1876.
periods.notes: Game: removal of the player-sultan only by palace coup/deposition (fetva of the Şeyhülislam) or death; ministers by royal dismissal.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire (First Constitutional Era)
periods.succession: Constitution of 1876 created an elected Chamber of Deputies, but ministers answered to the Sultan, who could exile anyone deemed dangerous (Art. 113 used against Midhat Pasha). Abdülhamid II prorogued parliament 14 Feb 1878.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire (Hamidian autocracy)
periods.succession: Personal rule of Abdülhamid II from Yıldız Palace; extensive informer network (jurnal system) rather than a formal intelligence agency.
periods.notes: Ended by the Young Turk Revolution (CUP), which forced restoration of the constitution.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire (Second Constitutional Era)
periods.succession: 1909 amendments made the cabinet responsible to the Chamber of Deputies; Abdülhamid II deposed after the 31 March Incident (Apr 1909). Military factions (CUP, Savior Officers 1912) repeatedly forced cabinets out.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire under CUP (Three Pashas)
periods.succession: Raid on the Sublime Porte (23 Jan 1913) brought the Committee of Union and Progress to power; from mid-1913 effective rule by Talat (Interior), Enver (War) and Cemal (Navy) Pashas; Sultan a figurehead.
periods.notes: Game: removal only by coup, military defeat or collapse (the triumvirs fled 2 Nov 1918).

periods.name: Ottoman Empire under Allied occupation (Istanbul government)
periods.capital: Constantinople (Istanbul) - occupied by the Allies (formally 16 Mar 1920)
periods.succession: Sultan Mehmed VI governed through grand viziers acceptable to the Allies; parliament dissolved Apr 1920. Overlaps with the rival Ankara government from Apr 1920.
periods.notes: Sultanate abolished 1 Nov 1922 by the Ankara Grand National Assembly; the last grand vizier resigned 4 Nov 1922.

periods.name: Government of the Grand National Assembly (Ankara)
periods.succession: Assembly government: the GNA elected each Commissar (Vekil) individually and the Speaker (Mustafa Kemal) chaired the Council of Executive Commissars; commissars could be voted out by the Assembly.
periods.notes: Game: a rival state to the Istanbul sultanate during the War of Independence (1919-1922); Treaty of Lausanne 24 Jul 1923.

periods.name: Republic of Turkey (single-party CHP era)
periods.succession: President elected by the GNA for the Assembly's term (no limit in practice); PM appointed by the President. Only the Republican People's Party (CHP) was permitted (brief opposition experiments 1924-25 and 1930).

periods.name: Republic of Turkey (multi-party democracy)
periods.succession: President elected by the GNA; government responsible to the GNA. Democrat Party governments 1950-1960.
periods.notes: Ended by the 27 May 1960 military coup.

periods.name: National Unity Committee (military junta)
periods.succession: Junta of 38 officers under Gen. Cemal Gürsel; new constitution 1961; PM Menderes, FM Zorlu and Finance Minister Polatkan executed.

periods.name: Second Republic (1961 constitution)
periods.succession: Bicameral GNA; President elected by GNA for 7 years. National Security Council gave the military a formal voice. 12 March 1971 'coup by memorandum' forced Demirel out and installed technocratic cabinets until 1973.
periods.notes: Game: elected government removable by no-confidence or by a military ultimatum (memorandum).

periods.name: National Security Council (military junta)
periods.succession: Gen. Kenan Evren and the service chiefs ruled as the NSC; 1982 constitution approved by referendum, Evren became president.

periods.name: Republic of Turkey (1982 constitution, parliamentary)
periods.succession: Unicameral GNA; PM and Council of Ministers responsible to the GNA. President elected by GNA (7 years) until 2014, then by popular vote (5 years). 28 February 1997 memorandum forced Erbakan out; 15 July 2016 coup attempt failed.

periods.name: Republic of Turkey (executive presidency)
periods.succession: 2017 referendum abolished the office of Prime Minister; the popularly elected President is head of state and government and appoints ministers (not MPs) without parliamentary confirmation. Two-term limit (a third if parliament calls an early election). Impeachment requires a 2/3 majority to send to the Constitutional Court.
periods.notes: Vice President: Cevdet Yılmaz (from 2023).
