role_notes.head_of_government: 1789-1922 Grand Vizier (Sadrazam), dismissed at the Sultan's will. 1920-23 the Ankara government had a Chairman of the Council of Executive Commissars (overlapping the Istanbul grand viziers). 1923-2018 Prime Minister (Başbakan). From 9 Jul 2018 the President heads the government.
role_notes.foreign: Before 1836 foreign affairs were run by the Reis ül-Küttab (Chief Scribe of the Imperial Council) - not listed; game should treat the Grand Vizier/Sultan as foreign-policy maker. Ottoman Foreign Ministers 1836-1922 are year-level (all flagged uncertain); short gaps exist. 1920-1923 Ankara foreign commissars listed.
role_notes.defense: No war ministry before 1826: the Grand Vizier commanded field armies and the Janissary Agha led the standing infantry - model as the Grand Vizier. 1826-1908 the Serasker (commander-in-chief/war minister); names are listed only from 1876 (1826-1876 seraskers not covered). 1908-1922 Minister of War (Harbiye Nazırı). Ankara/Republic: Minister of National Defence. Navy Ministry (Bahriye Nezareti) not listed.
role_notes.finance: Ottoman finance ministers 1838-1922 are INCOMPLETE (only those with dates in available lists; large gaps 1855-1860, 1863-1880, 1891-1908) - all flagged uncertain. Republic list complete.
role_notes.interior: Ottoman interior ministry existed 1836-1839 and again from 1869 (in between the functions sat with the Grand Vizier's deputy, Sadaret Kethüdası). Ottoman list is year-level and flagged uncertain.
role_notes.intelligence: No formal service before 1913 (Abdülhamid II used a palace informer network). 1913-1918 Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa (CUP special organisation). 1918-1926 Karakol/ad-hoc nationalist networks (not listed). 1926-1965 MAH; from 1965 MİT (Undersecretary, retitled President in 2017/18).
role_notes.military_chief: Ottoman Chief of the General Staff from 1908 (the Serasker served as the de facto army chief before). Republic: Chief of the General Staff (Genelkurmay Başkanı); answerable to the PM until 2018, to the Ministry of National Defence/President since.

uncertain: Ottoman grand viziers 1805 (Jun-Sep), 1809 and 1823-1824 have month-only or missing boundary dates.
Ottoman ministers 1836-1922 (foreign, interior, finance) are only year-precise and incomplete for finance; Mehmed Cavid Bey's three finance terms are from secondary sources.
Turkish Foreign Ministry 1956-1957 (after Köprülü's resignation) covered by acting ministers; Ethem Menderes entry uncertain.
Interior minister from Feb 2026 (Mustafa Çiftçi) taken from a recently updated list - verify.

nations.name: Russia (Russian Empire / USSR / Russian Federation)

periods.name: Russian Empire (autocracy)
periods.succession: Hereditary autocracy. From Paul I's Pauline Laws (Apr 1797) succession is by male primogeniture within the Romanov (Holstein-Gottorp) house. Emperors were removed only by death or palace coup (Paul I murdered by officers, Mar 1801) or assassination (Alexander II, Mar 1881). Ministers served and were dismissed at the emperor's pleasure; there was no parliament.
periods.notes: Ministries created by Alexander I's manifesto of Sep 1802 (replacing Peter the Great's colleges). The Committee of Ministers (from 1802) and State Council (1810) were advisory; there was no prime minister in the Western sense before Oct 1905. Coronations took place in Moscow, the 'second capital'.

military_chief: Count Hans Karl von Diebitsch (Ivan Dibich)

periods.name: Russian Empire (Duma monarchy)
periods.succession: October Manifesto (Oct 1905) and Fundamental Laws (May 1906) created an elected State Duma and a Council of Ministers under a chairman. Ministers remained responsible to the emperor, not the Duma; the Duma could not pass no-confidence votes (the emperor could dissolve it, as in 1906 and 1907). Nicholas II abdicated on 15 Mar 1917 (NS) during the February Revolution; his brother Michael declined the throne the next day.
periods.notes: Stolypin (PM) assassinated Sep 1911. Game: the Duma can only obstruct (budget, scandal); removal of the player is by revolution or forced abdication.

periods.name: Russian Provisional Government (Russian Republic from Sep 1917)
periods.succession: Self-appointed cabinet drawn from the Duma's Provisional Committee, sharing power with the Petrograd Soviet ('dual power'). No head of state; the minister-chairman acted for one. Overthrown by the Bolshevik October Revolution (7-8 Nov 1917 NS).
periods.notes: Kornilov affair (Sep 1917) = attempted military coup.

defense: Committee for Military and Naval Affairs (Vladimir Antonov-Ovseyenko, Nikolay Krylenko, Pavel Dybenko)

periods.name: Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (civil war)
periods.succession: Power held by the Bolshevik (RCP(b)) leadership through the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom); the Constituent Assembly was dispersed in Jan 1918. Left SRs left the coalition in Mar 1918, after which the state was effectively one-party. Rival White governments existed 1918-20 (Kolchak, Denikin, Wrangel).
periods.notes: Lenin was leader by authority, not by a party office; the post of General Secretary was created Apr 1922 (Stalin).

defense: Committee for Military and Naval Affairs (Vladimir Antonov-Ovseyenko, Nikolay Krylenko, Pavel Dybenko)

periods.name: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
periods.succession: Real power lay with the General (First) Secretary of the CPSU Central Committee and the Politburo. Leaders left office by death (Lenin, Stalin, Brezhnev, Andropov, Chernenko) or were removed by the Central Committee/Presidium (Khrushchev, Oct 1964; the 'Anti-Party Group' attempt failed in Jun 1957). State offices (Premier, Chairman of the Presidium) were often held by rivals or figureheads. Mar 1990: party's 'leading role' abolished and an executive Presidency created (Gorbachev, elected by the Congress of People's Deputies). Aug 1991 coup attempt (State Committee on the State of Emergency) failed; the USSR was dissolved 25-26 Dec 1991.
periods.notes: Game: the player is the General Secretary. No no-confidence or impeachment; removal by Politburo/Central Committee vote (party_congress), coup, or death. Head of state and head of government are advisors/rivals, not the player's office (except when the GS also held them: Stalin as premier 1941-53, Khrushchev 1958-64, Brezhnev/Andropov/Chernenko/Gorbachev as head of state).

periods.name: Russian Federation (transitional, 1978 RSFSR constitution as amended)
periods.succession: Directly elected president (Yeltsin, Jun 1991) in conflict with the Congress of People's Deputies/Supreme Soviet. The Sep-Oct 1993 constitutional crisis ended with Yeltsin dissolving parliament and shelling the White House; parliament's 'acting president' Rutskoy (22 Sep - 4 Oct 1993) was arrested.

periods.name: Russian Federation (1993 constitution)
periods.succession: President directly elected (4-year terms to 2012, 6-year since; two consecutive terms, 2020 amendments reset Putin's count, allowing him to serve to 2036). Impeachment requires Duma (2/3) + Supreme Court + Constitutional Court + Federation Council (2/3); attempted 1999, failed. The PM is nominated by the president and confirmed by the Duma (three rejections -> dissolution) and can be dismissed by the president at will. The Duma may pass no confidence, but the president may ignore the first vote and dissolve the Duma after a second. If the president dies or resigns, the PM becomes acting president (Putin, 31 Dec 1999).
periods.notes: Game: in practice a dominant-president system; model the president as the player's office. Removal mainly via election defeat, resignation, death, or elite coup.

role_notes.head_of_state: 1917-03 to 1917-11 there was no head of state; the Provisional Government's minister-chairman acted for one. Soviet heads of state (VTsIK/CEC/Presidium chairmen) were largely ceremonial; the General Secretary held power.
role_notes.head_of_government: Before 1810 the emperor presided over the Committee of Ministers himself; chairmen 1810-1864 had little power (dates approximate). Real head of government only from Oct 1905 (Witte).
role_notes.paramount_leader: Use this as the player's office for 1917-1991. General Secretary formally from Apr 1922; Stalin not undisputed until c.1929. Mar-Sep 1953 collective leadership (Malenkov premier, Khrushchev party).
role_notes.foreign: Before Sep 1802 foreign affairs were run by the College of Foreign Affairs under a (vice-)chancellor; dates for 1789-1802 are approximate.
role_notes.defense: Before Sep 1802: War College. 1917-18 collegial commissariat. The navy had a separate ministry 1802-1917 (see navy_minister) and a separate People's Commissariat of the Navy 1937-46 and 1950-53 (not listed).
role_notes.finance: No finance minister before Sep 1802: state finances were overseen by the Procurator-General of the Senate (see interior) and the State Treasurer.
role_notes.interior: Before 1802 the Procurator-General of the Senate acted as chief of internal administration. 1930-34 no all-union interior commissariat (OGPU handled policing). 1960-66 interior affairs handled by republican ministries only.
role_notes.intelligence: No dedicated political-police chief 1789-1810 (Secret Expedition of the Senate to 1801); Ministry of Police 1810-19; Third Section 1826-80; 1880-1917 Okhrana under the MVD Department of Police (game: use the Interior Minister). 1934-41 and 1941-43 state security was part of the NKVD, so the NKVD chief is listed. Post-1991 both FSB (domestic) and SVR (foreign) directors are listed; the GRU (military intelligence) chief is not.
role_notes.military_chief: 1789-1815 and 1832-1865 there was no separate general-staff chief: model the War Minister/field commander (e.g. Kutuzov 1812) as military chief. In WWI and 1917 the operational chief was the Supreme Commander/Stavka chief of staff rather than the GUGSh chief (who handled the rear). 1918-24 the Red Army's Commander-in-Chief (Glavkom) outranked the staff chiefs.

uncertain: All imperial dates are Gregorian (New Style) as given by rulers.org; contemporary Russian sources use Julian (Old Style) dates 11-13 days earlier.
1789-1802 college heads, 1810-1864 Committee of Ministers chairmen, Third Section chiefs and pre-1866 general-staff chiefs are from general reference knowledge; months approximate.

nations.name: Spain

periods.name: Kingdom of Spain - Bourbon absolute monarchy (Carlos IV)
periods.succession: Hereditary. The First Secretary of State (Primer Secretario de Estado y del Despacho) was the leading minister and also the foreign minister. Manuel Godoy dominated policy 1792-1808 (as First Secretary to 1798, then as royal favourite and Generalísimo).
periods.notes: The Mutiny of Aranjuez (17-19 Mar 1808) toppled Godoy and forced Carlos IV to abdicate in favour of Fernando VII; both then renounced the crown to Napoleon at Bayonne (May 1808).

periods.name: Reign of Isabel II (Royal Statute 1834; Constitutions of 1837 and 1845)
periods.succession: Hereditary; regencies of María Cristina (1833-40) and Espartero (1840-43). The crown appointed and dismissed the President of the Council; governments then 'made' elections. Military pronunciamientos (1836, 1840, 1843, 1854, 1866, 1868) were the main way governments changed against the crown's will.
periods.notes: First Carlist War 1833-1840 (rival claimant Carlos María Isidro). Isabel II deposed by the Glorious Revolution (Sep 1868).

periods.name: Bourbon Restoration (Constitution of 1876)
periods.succession: Hereditary (Alfonso XII; regency of María Cristina 1885-1902; Alfonso XIII). Turno pacífico: the king alternated Conservative and Liberal leaders in office, and the incoming government then manufactured an electoral majority (caciquismo). Governments fell when the crown withdrew confidence or the ruling party split.
periods.notes: Prime ministers Cánovas (1897), Canalejas (1912) and Dato (1921) were assassinated.

periods.name: Parliamentary monarchy (Constitution of 1978)
periods.succession: Hereditary monarch with no executive power. periods.notes: Failed military coup 23 Feb 1981 (23-F).

role_notes.head_of_state: Parallel claimants: Joseph I (1808-13) vs the Patriot Junta/Regency; Republic vs Nationalist zone (1936-39). Regents are listed as separate entries because they exercised the crown's powers. Carlist pretenders (1833-76) are not listed.
role_notes.head_of_government: Before 1834 the First Secretary of State (Primer Secretario de Estado y del Despacho) was the leading minister, but under the absolute monarchy the king (and, 1792-1808, the favourite Godoy) held real power; game should treat the king as player and the First Secretary as chief advisor. During the First Republic (Feb 1873 - Jan 1874) the President of the Executive Power combined both roles. The Patriot governments of 1808-1813 had secretaries of state who are not listed here (gap). Franco combined head of state and government 1938-1973.
role_notes.foreign: 1789-1834: First Secretaries of State (same persons as head_of_government). 1808-1813: rulers.org lists only Joseph I's foreign ministers (Bonapartist); the Patriot foreign secretaries are not covered. 1834-1931: year-level dates only (rulers.org foreign-minister list); month precision would need the official Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores list. 1931-2026: full dates (rulers.org); Civil War entries split Republican vs Nationalist (Burgos) governments.
role_notes.defense: Secretary of State / Minister of War 1807-1931 from es.wikipedia (cross-check grade; holders with overlapping dates are flagged uncertain). GAP 1789-1807: Carlos IV's war secretaries (e.g. conde de Campo Alange, Azanza, Álvarez, Cornel) are not included because dates could not be verified. 1931-39 War/National Defence; 1939-1977 there was no defence ministry - the Minister of the Army (Ejército) is listed; separate Navy (Marina) and Air (Aire) ministers are not. Ministry of Defence from Jul 1977.
role_notes.finance: Hacienda: 1785-1931 from es.wikipedia annex list (cross-check grade; overlaps flagged; a few obvious year typos corrected and noted); 1931-2026 from rulers.org. Some pre-1931 entries in the source duplicate two names for one cabinet - both kept and flagged.
role_notes.interior: Gobernación (Interior): GAP before Oct 1833 - the Secretaría de la Gobernación existed only 1812-1814 and 1820-1823 (not covered); Fomento/Interior 1832-1836, Gobernación 1836-1977, Interior since 1977. 1833-1931 from es.wikipedia (cross-check grade, incomplete in places, overlaps flagged), 1931-2026 from rulers.org.
role_notes.intelligence: No public national intelligence chief before 1977. Franco-era services (SIPM in the Civil War; SECED 1972-77 under Carrero Blanco) had chiefs who were not officially public. CESID directors 1977-2002 (year-level dates), CNI directors 2002-2026 (month-level).
role_notes.military_chief: No permanent chief of staff before 1904; the king was nominal commander-in-chief and the War Minister the senior military authority (game: use War Minister). Estado Mayor Central 1904-1931 chiefs are NOT covered (gap). Republic: Franco (1935-36), Martínez Cabrera, Rojo (approximate months, flagged). Nationalist/Francoist: Franco as Generalísimo, then Jefes del Alto Estado Mayor (1939-1980), Presidents of the Junta de Jefes de Estado Mayor (1977-1984), JEMAD (1984-).

uncertain: Pre-1931 Spanish ministers of war, finance and interior come from es.wikipedia annex lists (cross-check grade). Entries whose dates overlap another holder in the source are flagged uncertain=True; obvious year typos were corrected and noted.
Spanish foreign ministers 1834-1931 have year-level dates only.
1789-1807 war secretaries, 1808-1813 Patriot ministers, 1812-1833 Gobernación ministers and 1904-1931 chiefs of the Central General Staff are not covered.
Arcadi España as Minister of Finance from 26 Mar 2026 (replacing María Jesús Montero) and other 2025-26 changes are as given by rulers.org at cut-off; verify against lamoncloa.gob.es.
Republican and Nationalist chiefs of staff 1935-1939 have approximate months.

nations.name: United Kingdom

periods.name: Kingdom of Great Britain
periods.succession: Hereditary monarchy (male-preference primogeniture, Protestant under the Act of Settlement 1701). The King chooses the PM, who must also command the Commons; ministers serve at royal pleasure.
periods.notes: Monarch retains real political power: George III effectively dismissed the Fox-North coalition (1783) and the Talents ministry (1807). Electorate tiny; elections managed by patronage. Game: player as PM can be removed by royal dismissal or loss of Commons confidence.

military_chief: Prince Frederick, Duke of York and Albany

periods.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (pre-reform)
periods.succession: Act of Union 1800 merged the Irish Parliament into Westminster. Great Reform Act 1832 widened the franchise. William IV's dismissal of Melbourne (Nov 1834) was the last royal dismissal of a PM.
periods.notes: Spencer Perceval assassinated 1812. Regency 1811-1820.

periods.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
periods.succession: Monarch appoints whoever can command a Commons majority (by convention the majority party leader). Governments fall by losing a confidence vote, losing an election, or party revolt (e.g. Asquith replaced by Lloyd George Dec 1916, Lloyd George ousted by the Carlton Club meeting Oct 1922). Parliament Act 1911 curbed the Lords.
periods.notes: Franchise widened 1867, 1884, 1918 (women over 30), 1928 (equal franchise).

periods.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
periods.succession: Irish Free State left Dec 1922 (name formally changed 1927). PM is the leader of the majority party; a party leadership change installs a new PM without a general election (Eden 1955, Home 1963, Callaghan 1976, Major 1990, Brown 2007, May 2016, Johnson 2019, Truss and Sunak 2022, Burnham 2026). Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 repealed 2022.
periods.notes: Game: no impeachment. Remove a UK player via (a) Commons no-confidence vote (last successful 1979), (b) defeat at a general election (max 5-year term), (c) a party leadership challenge / cabinet revolt (Thatcher 1990, Johnson 2022, Truss 2022). Monarch is ceremonial; never a coup.

role_notes.head_of_government: Before 1905 'Prime Minister' was not an official title; the holder was First Lord of the Treasury (Salisbury was Lord Privy Seal/Foreign Secretary instead in some ministries).
role_notes.defense: 1789-1794: no cabinet war minister; the Secretary at War was an administrative office and war policy ran through the PM and Home Secretary. 1794-1801 Secretary of State for War; 1801-1854 War and the Colonies; 1854-1964 Secretary of State for War (army). 1940-46 the PM held the separate post of Minister of Defence; 1946-64 Minister of Defence coordinated the service ministries; from Apr 1964 a unified Secretary of State for Defence. During 1940-45 the War Secretaries (Eden, Margesson, Grigg) are not listed separately - Churchill is the defence advisor. The Royal Navy's political chief is in navy_minister (First Lord of the Admiralty, 1789-1964).
role_notes.intelligence: No intelligence service before Oct 1909 (Secret Service Bureau): the game should use the Foreign Secretary's secret-service fund / Home Office for 1789-1909. This list combines MI5 (domestic, title 'Director General of the Security Service') and SIS/MI6 (foreign, title 'Chief of the Secret Intelligence Service'). Names were officially secret until 1992 (MI5) / 1994 (SIS avowed by the Intelligence Services Act); the game may treat pre-1992 chiefs as 'unknown to the public'.
role_notes.military_chief: 1789-1904 Commander-in-Chief of the Forces (vacant 1789-92 and Apr-Aug 1827); 1904-1959 Chief of the (Imperial) General Staff - an army post that was de facto senior military advisor; from 1959 the Chief of the Defence Staff. The 1958-59 interval is covered by the Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee (Dickson).
role_notes.finance: Before 1830s the Chancellor of the Exchequer was often the PM himself (First Lord of the Treasury).

uncertain: 2026 changes (Starmer -> Burnham 20 Jul 2026; Healey resignation 11 Jun 2026; Jarvis, Streeting, Healey, Miliband appointments) post-date the model's knowledge and were verified against news reports and worldstatesmen.org only; re-check before shipping.
SIS chiefs 1968-1999: start/end months are approximate (SIS has published years only); flagged individually.
First Lords of the Admiralty: Lord Auckland's 1834 and 1835 tenures - months approximate.
Wellington's 1827-28 tenure as C-in-C was interrupted (Apr-Aug 1827 vacancy); simplified to one entry.
Secretary of State for War 1794: Henry Dundas listed from Jul 1794; Sir George Yonge's Secretary at War tenure (from 1782) included as context, not a true cabinet war minister.

nations.name: Argentina

periods.name: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Spanish)
periods.succession: Spanish viceroys.
periods.notes: British invasions 1806-07 repelled by local militia. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).

periods.name: United Provinces / Argentine Confederation (revolution, civil wars)
periods.succession: Juntas, Supreme Directors (1814-20), Rosas' Buenos Aires dictatorship (1829-32, 1835-52), Confederation under the 1853 Constitution (Urquiza, Derqui); Buenos Aires seceded 1852-61.
periods.notes: May Revolution 25 May 1810; independence 9 Jul 1816. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).

periods.name: Republic (Conservative order, then Radical governments)
periods.succession: President chosen by an electoral college for 6 years, no immediate re-election (1853 Constitution). Sáenz Peña Law (1912) introduced universal, secret, compulsory male suffrage; UCR won 1916.
periods.notes: Failed Radical revolutions 1890, 1893, 1905. Paraguayan War 1865-70. Mass immigration.

periods.name: Uriburu provisional military government
periods.succession: Coup of 6 Sep 1930 against Yrigoyen.
periods.notes: First of six successful 20th-century coups.

periods.name: 'Infamous Decade' (Concordancia)
periods.succession: Fraudulent elections returned Concordancia presidents.
periods.notes: Roca-Runciman Pact 1933; Argentina neutral in WWII until Mar 1945.

periods.name: GOU military government
periods.succession: Coup of 4 Jun 1943; presidents Rawson, Ramírez, Farrell; Perón rose as labour secretary, war minister and vice-president.
periods.notes: Perón arrested and freed by mass mobilisation 17 Oct 1945.

periods.name: Perón presidency
periods.succession: Elected 1946; 1949 Constitution allowed re-election (1951).
periods.notes: Increasingly authoritarian. Overthrown by the 'Revolución Libertadora' (16-21 Sep 1955).

periods.name: Revolución Libertadora (military)
periods.succession: Lonardi, then Aramburu (palace coup 13 Nov 1955). Peronism banned.

periods.name: Semi-democracy with Peronism proscribed
periods.succession: Frondizi (1958) deposed by the military 29 Mar 1962; Senate president Guido sworn in under military tutelage; Illia elected 1963, deposed 28 Jun 1966.

head_of_state: Revolutionary Junta (Pascual Pistarini; Benigno Ignacio Varela; Adolfo Teodoro Álvarez)

periods.name: 'Revolución Argentina' (military)
periods.succession: Junta of the three commanders appointed presidents (Onganía, Levingston, Lanusse) and removed them by internal coups (1970, 1971).
periods.notes: Cordobazo 1969; Montoneros and ERP guerrillas.

head_of_state: Revolutionary Junta (Pascual Pistarini; Benigno Ignacio Varela; Adolfo Teodoro Álvarez)

periods.name: Return of Peronism
periods.succession: Cámpora elected and resigned to allow new elections; Perón elected Sep 1973, died 1 Jul 1974; succeeded by Vice-President Isabel Perón.

head_of_state: Military junta (Jorge Rafael Videla; Emilio Eduardo Massera; Orlando Ramón Agosti)

periods.name: National Reorganization Process (military junta)
periods.succession: The Junta of the Army, Navy and Air Force commanders was the supreme organ; it appointed and replaced the President (Videla, Viola, Galtieri, Bignone). Game: 'junta_decision' = removal by the junta.
periods.notes: 'Dirty War' (est. 9,000-30,000 disappeared). Falklands/Malvinas War Apr-Jun 1982; defeat forced Galtieri out and a return to democracy.

head_of_state: Military junta (Jorge Rafael Videla; Emilio Eduardo Massera; Orlando Ramón Agosti)

periods.name: Democracy (1853 Constitution, reformed 1994)
periods.succession: Since 1994: direct two-round election, 4-year term, one consecutive re-election. Vice-president, then Senate provisional president, then the Legislative Assembly chooses a successor. The Chief of Cabinet (since 1994) is politically answerable to Congress and can be removed by an absolute-majority censure vote of either chamber (Art. 101).
periods.notes: Alfonsín handed over early (Jul 1989) amid hyperinflation. Dec 2001 crisis: De la Rúa resigned after riots (game: 'revolution'), followed by five presidents in two weeks. Juicio político (impeachment) has never removed a president.

role_notes.head_of_state: Presidential system: the President is head of state and of government. Holders are listed from 1862 (national reunification); tier-2 minimum is 1900. Military juntas appear as collective entries.
role_notes.head_of_government: The President is head of government. Listed here is the Chief of the Cabinet of Ministers (Jefe de Gabinete de Ministros, created by the 1994 reform), a coordinating minister who answers to Congress and can be removed by a censure (moción de censura) vote - the closest Argentine analogue to a no-confidence target.
role_notes.foreign: Ministro de Relaciones Exteriores y Culto (title varied: '... Comercio Internacional y Culto' 1992-2023). Brief acting stand-ins during a minister's absence (<45 days) are omitted.
role_notes.defense: Minister of War (Ministro de Guerra) to 1949, Minister of National Defence (Ministro de Defensa Nacional / de Defensa) from 1949; a separate Navy Ministry (Marina) existed 1898-1958. Sep 1955 - Jun 1958 no Defence minister: the Army, Navy and Air Force ministers (members of the governing junta) reported directly to the president.
role_notes.finance: Ministro de Hacienda to 1950s; Economía (various combined names) thereafter; Hacienda y Finanzas Públicas / Hacienda Dec 2015 - Dec 2019 (Macri abolished the Economy ministry; Finanzas split off Jan 2017 - Jun 2018 under Luis Caputo, not listed).
role_notes.interior: Ministro del Interior (from 2012 'del Interior y Transporte', 2015-19 'del Interior, Obras Públicas y Vivienda'). Security was split off to a separate Ministerio de Seguridad from Dec 2010 (Nilda Garré, Patricia Bullrich, ...). rulers.org shows the Interior portfolio ending 3 Jul 2026 when Diego Santilli moved to Chief of Cabinet - status after that not verified.
role_notes.intelligence: SIDE (Secretaría de Informaciones del Estado / de Inteligencia del Estado) 1946-2015; Agencia Federal de Inteligencia (AFI) 2015-2024 (mostly run by 'interventores' 2019-24); SIDE re-created Jul 2024. Heads report directly to the president.
role_notes.military_chief: Chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces (Jefe del Estado Mayor Conjunto, created 1948/49; minor role under the juntas). During military regimes real power lay with the Army, Navy and Air Force commanders-in-chief who formed the junta. No joint chief before 1949.

uncertain: Ministers before 25 May 1973 come from es.wikipedia tables (Interior, Foreign, Defence/War, Hacienda/Economía - the last derived from the Economy Ministry's official CDI list); from 1973 from rulers.org's Argentine ministries page.
Brief acting stand-ins (<45 days) and interim holders nested inside a minister's term are omitted.
Defence Sep 1955 - Jun 1958 and Interior/Finance overlaps in the 1955-58 and 1966 juntas may be incomplete.

2025-26 changes (Cabinet chiefs Adorni Nov 2025 and Santilli Jun 2026; Defence minister Carlos Presti Dec 2025; Joint Staff chief Dalle Nogare Dec 2025; Security minister Monteoliva Dec 2025; SIDE heads after Jul 2024) are from rulers.org / es.wikipedia and were not checked against the Boletín Oficial.

nations.name: Australia

periods.name: Commonwealth of Australia (Melbourne seat of government)
periods.succession: Westminster system: Governor-General commissions the leader able to command the House of Representatives. Unstable three-party parliaments 1901-1910 saw governments fall on the floor of the House (Deakin 1904, Watson 1904, Reid 1905, Deakin 1908, Fisher 1909). Hughes expelled from Labor over conscription (1916) and formed the Nationalist Party.
periods.notes: Foreign policy formally under London until the 1926 Balfour Declaration; Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster only in 1942 (backdated to 1939).

periods.name: Commonwealth of Australia (Canberra)
periods.succession: PM is the leader of the majority party/coalition in the House. Party-room 'leadership spills' are the most common removal: Menzies 1941 (lost party support), Gorton 1971 (tied party vote), Hawke 1991, Rudd 2010, Gillard 2013, Abbott 2015, Turnbull 2018. Unique reserve-power removal: Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed Whitlam on 11 Nov 1975 after the Senate blocked supply. Lyons (1939), Curtin (1945) and Holt (1967) died in office.
periods.notes: Parliament moved to Canberra 9 May 1927. Australia Acts 1986 ended residual UK legal links. 1999 republic referendum failed - the monarch remains head of state, represented by the Governor-General.

nations.name: Cuba

periods.name: Spanish colony (Captaincy General of Cuba)
periods.succession: Captains-general appointed by the Spanish Crown.
periods.notes: Independence wars: Ten Years' War 1868-78, Little War 1879-80, War of Independence 1895-98 (insurgent 'Republic in Arms' governments). Spanish-American War 1898. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).

periods.name: First U.S. military occupation
periods.succession: U.S. military governors (Brooke, Wood).
periods.notes: Platt Amendment (1901) incorporated in the Cuban constitution: U.S. right of intervention and Guantánamo lease (1903).

periods.name: Republic of Cuba (Platt Amendment protectorate)
periods.succession: 1901 Constitution: president elected indirectly for 4 years.
periods.notes: Estrada Palma's disputed re-election triggered the 1906 'August Revolution' and U.S. intervention.

periods.name: Second U.S. occupation (Provisional Government)
periods.succession: U.S. provisional governors (Taft, Magoon).

periods.name: Republic (Liberal/Conservative alternation; Machado dictatorship)
periods.succession: Indirect election, 4-year terms; Machado extended his term to 1935 via the 1928 'prórroga de poderes'.
periods.notes: U.S. landings 1912 (Race War) and 1917 (Chambelona revolt). Machado (1925-33) became dictatorial; overthrown by a general strike, army defection and U.S. mediation, Aug 1933.

nations.name: Egypt

periods.name: Khedivate of Egypt (Ottoman suzerainty, British occupation)
periods.succession: Khedivate hereditary in the Muhammad Ali dynasty (primogeniture since 1866 firman).
periods.notes: Real power lay with the British Agent and Consul-General (Cromer 1883-1907, Gorst 1907-11, Kitchener 1911-14). Ministers were appointed by the khedive with British approval; PM Boutros Ghali assassinated 1910. Game: semi-playable client state - foreign and military policy dictated by Britain.

periods.name: Sultanate of Egypt (British protectorate)
periods.succession: Britain deposed Khedive Abbas II (19 Dec 1914) and installed his uncle Hussein Kamel as Sultan.
periods.notes: British High Commissioner held real power. 1919 Revolution led by the Wafd; protectorate ended by unilateral British declaration of 28 Feb 1922.

periods.name: Kingdom of Egypt
periods.succession: Hereditary monarchy (Fuad I, Farouk). 1923 constitution: PM responsible to parliament, but the king could dismiss governments and dissolve parliament, and repeatedly did so against Wafd majorities. Britain intervened directly (Abdeen Palace incident, 4 Feb 1942, tanks forced Farouk to appoint Nahhas).
periods.notes: Britain retained reserved points (defence, Suez, Sudan, foreigners) until the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty; troops in the Canal Zone until 1956. Two PMs assassinated (Ahmad Maher 1945, Nokrashy 1948).

periods.name: Kingdom under the Free Officers (regency for Fuad II)
periods.succession: Free Officers coup of 23 Jul 1952 forced Farouk to abdicate (26 Jul) for infant Fuad II; Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) ruled.
periods.notes: Monarchy abolished 18 Jun 1953.

periods.name: Republic of Egypt / United Arab Republic (1958-61 union with Syria; name kept to 1971)
periods.succession: RCC power struggle: Nasser ousted Naguib (Feb-Nov 1954). President nominated by the National Assembly and confirmed by plebiscite (1956 constitution). Single party: Liberation Rally -> National Union -> Arab Socialist Union.
periods.notes: Military-backed presidential authoritarianism. Defeat in 1967 led to Nasser's (rejected) resignation offer and the purge of Field Marshal Amer.

periods.name: Arab Republic of Egypt (1971 constitution)
periods.succession: People's Assembly nominates, referendum confirms (multi-candidate election from 2005). Vice-president succeeded (Sadat 1970, Mubarak 1981). Sadat assassinated 6 Oct 1981. Mubarak forced out by the 25 January Revolution (11 Feb 2011), with SCAF taking power.
periods.notes: Dominant-party system (NDP from 1978). PM appointed and dismissed by the president; parliament never toppled a government.

periods.name: Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (transition)
periods.succession: SCAF chairman Tantawi exercised presidential powers until the elected president took office.

periods.name: Arab Republic of Egypt (Morsi presidency)
periods.succession: Direct presidential election (Jun 2012).
periods.notes: Morsi removed by the military on 3 Jul 2013 after mass protests - the canonical 'coup' removal.

periods.name: Arab Republic of Egypt (2014 constitution; Sisi era)
periods.capital: Cairo (government relocating to the New Administrative Capital from 2023)
periods.succession: Interim president Adly Mansour 2013-14; direct presidential elections 2014, 2018, 2023. 2019 amendments extended terms to six years and allow Sisi to serve to 2030.
periods.notes: Military-dominated presidential system. PM appointed by the president with parliamentary approval; House can withdraw confidence but has never done so.

role_notes.head_of_state: Pre-1914 the Ottoman Sultan was nominal suzerain and the British Consul-General (Cromer, Gorst, Kitchener) the real power; 1914-1936 British High Commissioners (McMahon, Wingate, Allenby, Lloyd, Loraine, Lampson) wielded a veto. Game: model a 'foreign overseer' advisor who can force dismissal.
role_notes.foreign: No Egyptian foreign minister before 1922 (foreign relations handled by Ottoman Porte/Britain; a nominal portfolio held by Adly Yakan and Rushdi 1914-17). Many PMs 1923-52 also held Foreign Affairs.
role_notes.defense: Before 1952 the War Ministry was subordinate to the British-officered army (Sirdar until 1924; British Military Mission to 1947); ministers changed with every cabinet and are not listed here. Game: use the PM/king as defence authority pre-1952. After 1952 the War/Defence minister is always a senior officer and the key coup-maker.
role_notes.finance: Pre-1952 finance ministers rotated with cabinets (Makram Ebeid for most Wafd governments, 1928-44); not listed due to incomplete dates.
role_notes.interior: Pre-1952 the Interior portfolio was usually held by the Prime Minister himself (e.g. Nahhas, Sidqi, Nokrashy). Game: PM doubles as interior minister before 1952. 1962-65 holder(s) not confirmed.
role_notes.intelligence: General Intelligence Service (al-Mukhabarat al-Amma) founded 1954. Military Intelligence and State Security Investigations (Interior Ministry; renamed National Security Agency 2011) are separate.
role_notes.military_chief: Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces from 1952. Under the monarchy the British Sirdar (to 1924) then Egyptian Chiefs of Staff (e.g. Ibrahim Atallah in 1948) - not listed.

uncertain: Foreign ministers 1933-1952: Wikipedia gives years only and the order of very short 1952 tenures is unclear.
War ministers 1952-54 overlap in sources (Naguib/Boghdadi/Amer/el-Shafei).

February 2026 reshuffle: Wikipedia names Ashraf Salem Zaher as defence minister from 11 Feb 2026, while Al Jazeera reported defence unchanged. Finance (Kouchouk) and Interior (Tawfik) assumed retained.
GIS directors 1954-1993: years only.
Interior ministers 1953-1977: years only; 1962-65 gap.

periods.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands (royal government)
periods.capital: Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government at The Hague
periods.succession: King William I (abdicated 1840) and William II governed personally; ministers answered to the King. Belgium seceded 1830-1839.

periods.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary monarchy)
periods.capital: Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government at The Hague
periods.succession: Thorbecke's 1848 constitution made ministers responsible to the States General; ministerial responsibility to parliament settled by 1868. Hereditary House of Orange-Nassau (female succession from 1890). Proportional representation from 1917/1918.
periods.notes: The prime ministership was a rotating chairmanship of the Council of Ministers until 1901 and a permanent post only from 1937/1945.

defense: George August Alexander Alting von Geusau

periods.name: German occupation; government-in-exile in London
periods.capital: London (government-in-exile); occupied territory under Reichskommissar Arthur Seyss-Inquart
periods.succession: Queen Wilhelmina and the cabinet governed from London; the Queen dismissed PM De Geer in Sep 1940. Occupied Netherlands ruled by Reichskommissar Seyss-Inquart.
periods.notes: Game: the exile government remains the playable Dutch government, without control of the homeland.

periods.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary democracy)
periods.capital: Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government, parliament and monarch at The Hague
periods.succession: Multi-party coalition governments formed after negotiation (formateur/informateur). A cabinet or minister that loses the confidence of the Tweede Kamer (motion of no confidence or censure) resigns and stays on as caretaker (demissionair) until a successor cabinet is sworn in - hence long caretaker periods (e.g. Rutte IV 2023-24, Schoof 2025-26).
periods.notes: Decolonisation: Indonesia 1949, Suriname 1975. Founding member of NATO and the EEC.

role_notes.head_of_government: Holders' end dates are the swearing-in of the successor cabinet; outgoing cabinets serve as caretakers (demissionair) in between.
role_notes.defense: Minister of War (army) and a separate Minister of the Navy (not listed) until 1928, and again 1941-1959 (often held by one person, e.g. Staf 1951-59); Minister of Defence 1928-1941 and from 1959. Pre-1928 War ministers are year-level within cabinets (flagged).
role_notes.intelligence: No public national security chief before 1945 (the interwar Centrale Inlichtingendienst was secret). BVD (domestic security) 1949-2002, AIVD from 2002; the military service MIVD (not listed) is separate. Foreign intelligence IDB existed 1946-1994 (not listed).
role_notes.military_chief: No permanent supreme commander in peacetime before 1949: the Opperbevelhebber was appointed for mobilisations (1914-1919, 1939-1940). 1949-1976 Chairman of the Combined Chiefs of Staff; 1976-2005 Chief of the Defence Staff; from 2005 Commandant der Strijdkrachten (CDS). Inter-war army chiefs of the General Staff not listed.

nations.name: Pakistan

periods.name: Dominion of Pakistan
periods.succession: Governor-General (representing the British monarch) held strong reserve powers and actually dismissed PM Nazimuddin (1953) and the Constituent Assembly (1954). PM chosen from the Muslim League majority.
periods.notes: Use 'royal_dismissal' for Governor-General dismissal of the PM. Includes East Bengal (East Pakistan).

periods.name: Islamic Republic of Pakistan (1956 constitution)
periods.succession: President Iskander Mirza appointed and removed four PMs in two years; ended by Mirza's martial law (7 Oct 1958) and Ayub Khan's coup against Mirza (27 Oct 1958).

periods.name: Military rule (Ayub Khan, then Yahya Khan)
periods.succession: Ayub ruled under martial law then the 1962 presidential constitution (indirect 'Basic Democracies' election 1965); forced out by mass protests and handed power to army chief Yahya Khan (Mar 1969). Yahya resigned after the loss of East Pakistan (Bangladesh) in the Dec 1971 war.
periods.notes: Model 1962-69 as presidential under military tutelage. No-confidence not available.

periods.name: Bhutto civilian government
periods.succession: Bhutto was civilian Chief Martial Law Administrator and President, then PM under the 1973 constitution (parliamentary, ceremonial president). Overthrown by army chief Zia-ul-Haq (Operation Fair Play, 5 Jul 1977); executed 1979.
periods.notes: Presidential system to Aug 1973.

periods.name: Zia-ul-Haq military rule
periods.succession: Martial law until Dec 1985; Zia President from 1978 and remained COAS. 8th Amendment (1985) gave the President Art. 58(2)(b) power to dismiss the PM and dissolve the National Assembly. Ended with Zia's death in an air crash (17 Aug 1988).
periods.notes: Non-party elections 1985 produced PM Junejo, whom Zia dismissed in May 1988.

periods.name: Restored parliamentary democracy
periods.succession: President used 58(2)(b) to dismiss Benazir Bhutto (1990, 1996) and Nawaz Sharif (1993; restored by Supreme Court, then both he and the president resigned under army pressure). Caretaker PMs govern during elections. 13th Amendment (1997) removed 58(2)(b). Ended by Musharraf's coup (12 Oct 1999).
periods.notes: Army chief is the decisive veto player ('troika' of President, PM, COAS).

periods.name: Musharraf military-led government
periods.succession: Musharraf 'Chief Executive' then President (2001, referendum 2002), retaining COAS until Nov 2007. 17th Amendment restored 58(2)(b). Civilian PMs from Nov 2002 under his supervision. Resigned Aug 2008 facing impeachment by the new parliament.
periods.notes: 2007 emergency rule and lawyers' movement.

periods.name: Islamic Republic of Pakistan (18th Amendment parliamentary system)
periods.succession: President elected by Parliament and provincial assemblies; 18th Amendment (2010) abolished the president's power to dismiss the PM. PMs removed by Supreme Court disqualification (Gilani 2012, Nawaz Sharif 2017) and by the first successful no-confidence vote (Imran Khan, 10 Apr 2022). Caretaker governments run elections.
periods.notes: Game: add 'judicial disqualification' as a removal event (map to impeachment). Army remains the dominant power: 27th Amendment (Nov 2025) created Chief of Defence Forces (held by Field Marshal Asim Munir), lifetime field-marshal rank immunity, and a Federal Constitutional Court.

nations.name: Poland

periods.name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
periods.succession: Elective monarchy (king chosen by the nobility); Constitution of 3 May 1791 sought a hereditary constitutional monarchy. Destroyed by the Second (1793) and Third (1795) Partitions; Stanisław August abdicated Nov 1795. Kościuszko Uprising 1794.

periods.name: Partitioned (Russia, Prussia, Austria); Duchy of Warsaw 1807-15; Congress Kingdom under Russia 1815-1915
periods.succession: No sovereign Polish state. Duchy of Warsaw (1807-15) was a Napoleonic client ruled by the King of Saxony; the Congress Kingdom (1815-) had the Russian emperor as king and lost its autonomy after the uprisings of 1830-31 and 1863-64. German/Austrian-sponsored Kingdom of Poland 1916-18 under a Regency Council. Not playable before Nov 1918.

head_of_state: Regency Council (Aleksander Kakowski, Zdzisław Lubomirski, Józef Ostrowski)

periods.name: Second Polish Republic (parliamentary)
periods.succession: Piłsudski Chief of State to Dec 1922, then presidents elected by the National Assembly (Sejm + Senate) for 7 years; President Narutowicz assassinated Dec 1922. Weak, short-lived coalition cabinets dependent on the Sejm (March Constitution 1921). Ended by Piłsudski's May Coup (12-15 May 1926).

head_of_state: Regency Council (Aleksander Kakowski, Zdzisław Lubomirski, Józef Ostrowski)

periods.name: Second Republic under Sanacja (Piłsudski regime)
periods.succession: Constitutional forms kept but real power with Marshal Piłsudski (minister of military affairs throughout, PM 1926-28 and 1930); PMs were his appointees, replaced at his will (model as 'royal_dismissal' by the strongman). Opposition persecuted (Brest trials 1930-32).

periods.name: Second Republic (April Constitution, authoritarian presidential)
periods.succession: April 1935 constitution concentrated power in the president (Mościcki), who appointed and dismissed the PM. After Piłsudski's death (May 1935) power was shared by Mościcki, Marshal Rydz-Śmigły and PM Składkowski. Ended by the German and Soviet invasions (Sep 1939).

periods.name: Government-in-exile (Angers, then London from 1940)
periods.succession: Constitutional continuity under the April Constitution: the president in exile designated his successor. Recognized by the Western Allies until 5 Jul 1945; afterwards largely symbolic until it handed the presidential insignia to Wałęsa in Dec 1990. Poland itself was occupied by Germany (General Government, annexed areas) and the USSR (1939-41).
periods.notes: Game: 1939-44/45 the playable Polish government is the London exile government (armed forces in exile, Home Army).

periods.name: Polish People's Republic (from 1952; Committee of National Liberation / Provisional Government 1944-47)
periods.succession: Soviet-backed regime (PKWN, Lublin, Jul 1944); rigged elections Jan 1947. Power with the First Secretary of the PPR/PZPR (paramount_leader) and Politburo, subject to Moscow. Leaders were replaced by Central Committee plenums after crises (Oct 1956 Gomułka's return; Dec 1970 Gierek after Baltic coast riots; Sep 1980 Kania after the Solidarity strikes; Oct 1981 Jaruzelski). Martial law 13 Dec 1981 - Jul 1983 under the Military Council of National Salvation (WRON, a military junta in all but name). Round Table talks and semi-free elections (Jun 1989) ended the regime.

periods.name: Third Polish Republic
periods.succession: President directly elected since 1990 (5-year term, max two), with a legislative veto (3/5 Sejm override) and influence over defence/foreign policy. Government headed by the Prime Minister (President of the Council of Ministers, Prezes Rady Ministrów), responsible to the Sejm; since the 1997 constitution only a constructive vote of no confidence can remove the cabinet. President may be tried by the State Tribunal (impeachment) on indictment by 2/3 of the National Assembly.
periods.notes: Semi-presidential features (cohabitation e.g. Duda vs Tusk 2023-25; Nawrocki vs Tusk 2025-). Game: player = PM; president is a veto player.

role_notes.head_of_state: 1795-1918 no Polish head of state (partition; Duchy of Warsaw ruled by Frederick Augustus I of Saxony 1807-15; Russian emperors as kings of Congress Poland). 1939-45 two rival claims: London exile presidents (internationally recognized to Jul 1945) and the communist KRN (from 1944). 1952-89 collective Council of State.
role_notes.paramount_leader: Use the PZPR First Secretary as the player's office 1944/47-1989. Dec 1981 - Jul 1983 Jaruzelski also chaired the WRON military council (martial law).
role_notes.head_of_government: London exile PMs (1939-90) and Lublin/Warsaw communist PMs (1944-) overlap; select by the player's chosen government. Sanacja-era PMs (1926-35) were subordinate to Piłsudski.
role_notes.defense: 1926-35 Piłsudski personally held the military affairs ministry; the Inspector General of the Armed Forces was the wartime commander-designate.
role_notes.intelligence: 1918-39 no civilian intelligence chief; military intelligence was Section II (Oddział II) of the General Staff (chiefs not listed). 1956-90 the SB was part of the Interior Ministry (use interior). Since 2002 ABW = domestic security; Foreign Intelligence Agency (AW) chiefs not listed.
role_notes.military_chief: Second Republic: Chief of the General Staff (Main Staff from 1928) served under the Inspector General of the Armed Forces (Piłsudski 1926-35, Rydz-Śmigły 1935-39), who is arguably the real military chief in war.

periods.name: ROC on Taiwan: KMT one-party martial-law state
periods.succession: President elected by the National Assembly (members frozen since 1947-48); Chiang Kai-shek re-elected until death; Temporary Provisions suspended term limits. Martial law 1949-05 to 1987-07.
periods.notes: Claimed to be the government of all China; UN seat until 1971-10.

periods.name: ROC: democratic transition
periods.notes: Opposition DPP legalized; National Assembly and Legislative Yuan fully re-elected 1991-92.

periods.name: ROC (Taiwan): democratic semi-presidential republic
periods.succession: President directly elected for 4 years (max two terms); appoints the Premier without legislative consent since 1997. Legislative Yuan can pass no-confidence against the Premier (president may then dissolve the legislature). Presidential recall/impeachment requires supermajorities.
periods.notes: Game: president removable by election/recall/impeachment; premier by presidential dismissal or no-confidence.

nations.name: Saudi Arabia

periods.name: Emirate of Riyadh / Nejd (Third Saudi State)
periods.succession: Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh (15 Jan 1902) from the Rashidis; his father Abdul Rahman kept the honorific of Imam. Rule by conquest and tribal allegiance (bay'ah).
periods.notes: Under British protection treaty (Darin, Dec 1915). No ministries: the ruler governs through family, ulema and tribal shaykhs.

head_of_state: Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)

periods.name: Sultanate of Nejd; Kingdom of Hejaz (1926) and Nejd (1927)
periods.succession: Hereditary by royal designation; conquest of Hejaz 1924-25. Prince Faisal served as Viceroy of the Hejaz from 1926 and presided over its Council of Deputies.
periods.notes: Treaty of Jeddah (May 1927) - British recognition of full independence. A Ministry of Foreign Affairs was created in Dec 1930 under Faisal.

head_of_state: Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)
Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)

periods.name: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (pre-Council of Ministers)
periods.succession: Agnatic seniority among sons of Abdulaziz; crown prince named by the king (Saud named 1933).
periods.notes: Only a handful of ministries existed (Foreign Affairs 1930, Finance 1932, Defence 1944, Interior 1951). The king was his own head of government; worldstatesmen lists Faisal as head of the Hejaz council 1932-53 but there was no national prime minister.

head_of_state: Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)
Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)

periods.name: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Council of Ministers era)
periods.succession: Council of Ministers founded 9 Oct 1953. Succession by agnatic seniority among Abdulaziz's sons, ratified by senior princes and the ulema (bay'ah). Saud was deposed in Nov 1964 by a family council backed by an ulema fatwa - the canonical 'family_council' removal. King Faisal was assassinated by a nephew in Mar 1975.
periods.notes: The king is normally also President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister).

head_of_state: Abdulaziz ibn Abdul Rahman Al Saud (Ibn Saud)

periods.name: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Basic Law)
periods.succession: Basic Law of Governance (Mar 1992) opens succession to grandsons of Abdulaziz; Allegiance Council created 2006. Crown princes have been replaced by royal order (Muqrin, Apr 2015; Muhammad bin Nayef, Jun 2017) - the game should model crown-prince removal as royal_dismissal rather than a vote.
periods.notes: No legislature with confidence powers (the Consultative/Shura Council, 1993, is appointed and advisory). In Sep 2022 King Salman appointed Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Prime Minister, the first time since 1953-54/1960-62 that the king did not personally chair the cabinet.

role_notes.head_of_government: No prime minister before 9 Oct 1953: the king ruled personally (game: king fills both offices). Since 1953 the king has normally chaired the Council of Ministers himself (game: one person, two offices), except Faisal 1954-60/1962-64 and MBS since Sep 2022.
role_notes.foreign: Faisal ran foreign affairs from 1926 (Hejaz) and formally from Dec 1930; before that Abdulaziz conducted diplomacy personally, largely with British agents.
role_notes.defense: No ministry before 1943/44; Abdulaziz commanded the Ikhwan and tribal levies himself. The game should treat the king as defence minister pre-1944.
role_notes.finance: Before 1932 the royal treasury (Bayt al-Mal) was run by Abdullah al-Sulaiman as the king's agent.
role_notes.interior: No interior ministry before 1951 (a short-lived Hejaz interior function under Faisal 1931-34 is sometimes cited). Regional emirs governed provinces.
role_notes.intelligence: General Intelligence Presidency (al-Ri'asa al-Amma lil-Istikhbarat) founded 1955. Before then: no public intelligence chief.
role_notes.military_chief: Chiefs of the General Staff before ~2014 are poorly documented in open sources; the defence minister (a senior prince) was the effective military chief. Game: use the defence minister as military chief pre-2014. Separate Saudi Arabian National Guard (commanded by Abdullah 1962-2010, Mutaib bin Abdullah 2010-17, Abdullah bin Bandar 2017-) answers directly to the king.

uncertain: Interior ministers 1951-1962: Wikipedia gives years only; months unverified.
GIP presidents 1955-2001: years only; Kamal Adham/Turki al-Faisal handover given as 1977 or 1979.
Sultan bin Abdulaziz's appointment as defence minister: Oct 1962 (Faisal cabinet) vs 1 Nov 1963 (Wikipedia list).
Chief of the General Staff pre-2018 incomplete; Al-Ruwaili still in office as of 2026-10 assumed (last confirmed Aug 2024).

nations.name: South Africa

periods.name: Boer republics (to 1902) and British colonies (Cape, Natal, Transvaal, Orange River Colony)
periods.succession: Second Boer War: the South African Republic (Transvaal, President Paul Kruger) and Orange Free State (President M.T. Steyn) annexed by Britain in 1900; Treaty of Vereeniging 31 May 1902. Colonies under British governors; responsible government restored to Transvaal (1906, PM Louis Botha) and ORC (1907).
periods.notes: Not a unified playable state before 31 May 1910. Game: treat as British colonial territory.

periods.name: Union of South Africa
periods.succession: British monarch represented by a Governor-General; PM is leader of the majority in the House of Assembly (white electorate; limited Coloured/Black franchise in the Cape, removed 1936/1956). Sovereign independence confirmed by the Statute of Westminster (1931) and Status of the Union Act (1934).
periods.notes: Smuts' government lost a parliamentary vote on entering WWII (Sep 1939), Hertzog resigned - Smuts became PM. National Party in power from 1948 (apartheid).

periods.name: Republic of South Africa (Westminster-style)
periods.succession: Ceremonial State President elected by Parliament (7-year term). PM = leader of the National Party caucus. Verwoerd assassinated in Parliament (6 Sep 1966); Vorster resigned in the Information Scandal (1978).
periods.notes: Left the Commonwealth on becoming a republic. Apartheid one-party dominance with white-only elections.

periods.name: Republic of South Africa (Tricameral constitution, executive State President)
periods.succession: 1983 constitution merged PM and State President into an executive State President elected by an electoral college of the tricameral Parliament. P.W. Botha was forced to resign by his cabinet (Aug 1989) after losing the NP leadership to F.W. de Klerk.
periods.notes: Negotiated transition 1990-94 (CODESA); Mandela released Feb 1990.

periods.name: Republic of South Africa (democratic, 1996 constitution)
periods.succession: Executive President elected by the National Assembly after each general election; max two terms. Removal: s.102 no-confidence vote (simple majority) or s.89 removal (two-thirds). In practice the ANC 'recalls' presidents: Mbeki resigned Sep 2008 after the ANC NEC recall; Zuma resigned Feb 2018 under threat of a no-confidence vote after losing the ANC presidency to Ramaphosa.
periods.notes: ANC lost its majority in May 2024; Government of National Unity (ANC, DA, IFP and others) formed June 2024. Head of state and government are the same person.

role_notes.head_of_state: 1910-61 the British monarch was represented by a Governor-General (Gladstone, Buxton, Prince Arthur of Connaught, Athlone, Clarendon, Duncan, de Wet (acting), van Zyl, Jansen, Steyn (acting), Swart). Since 1984 head of state and government are one office.
role_notes.foreign: 1910-1927 foreign relations were conducted by the British Foreign Office/Colonial Office through the PM's office. 1927-1955 the PM was also Minister of External Affairs.
role_notes.interior: Interior (to 1984), Internal Affairs (1984-85), Home Affairs (from 1985). Police/security was a separate Justice / Law and Order (Police) portfolio - for repression events the game may prefer the Minister of Justice/Police (e.g. B.J. Vorster 1961-66, Louis le Grange 1982-86, Adriaan Vlok 1986-91).
role_notes.intelligence: No civilian foreign intelligence service before BOSS (1969); the Security Branch of the police handled internal security. Post-2009 ministers responsible: Intelligence/State Security ministers (Ronnie Kasrils 2004-08, Siyabonga Cwele 2009-14, David Mahlobo 2014-17), then the Minister in the Presidency from 2021.
role_notes.military_chief: Union Defence Force (1912-57) -> South African Defence Force (1957-94) -> SANDF (1994-). Before 1920 the UDF had no single professional chief (Citizen Force Commandant-General C.F. Beyers resigned 1914 to lead the Maritz rebellion).

nations.name: South Korea (Republic of Korea)

periods.name: Joseon Kingdom
periods.notes: Qing tributary state; 'Hermit Kingdom'. Opened by the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876. Ministers not modeled (tier 2).

periods.name: Korean Empire
periods.succession: Emperor Gojong (1897-1907, forced to abdicate by Japan), Emperor Sunjong (1907-1910).
periods.notes: Japanese protectorate from 1905 (Eulsa Treaty); annexed 1910-08-29. Cabinet (Uijeongbu) not modeled.

periods.name: Japanese Korea (Chōsen)
periods.notes: Japanese Governor-General. Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in exile (Shanghai/Chongqing) 1919-45: not playable.

periods.name: United States Army Military Government in Korea
periods.notes: South of the 38th parallel.

periods.name: First Republic
periods.succession: President elected by the National Assembly (1948), then directly (1952 amendment). Rhee removed term limits for himself (1954).
periods.notes: Korean War 1950-53. Ended by the April Revolution after rigged 1960 election.

periods.name: Second Republic
periods.succession: Prime Minister (Chang Myon) responsible to the bicameral National Assembly; ceremonial president.
periods.notes: Overthrown by Park Chung-hee's 16 May 1961 coup.

periods.name: Military junta (Supreme Council for National Reconstruction)
periods.succession: SCNR Chairman (Chang Do-yong, then Park Chung-hee from 1961-07).

periods.name: Third Republic
periods.notes: Park elected 1963, 1967, 1971 (third term after 1969 amendment).

periods.name: Fourth Republic (Yushin) and 1979-80 transition
periods.succession: President chosen by the rubber-stamp National Conference for Unification; unlimited terms.
periods.notes: Park assassinated 1979-10-26; Chun Doo-hwan's 12.12 coup (1979) and the Gwangju massacre (1980-05).

periods.name: Fifth Republic
periods.succession: President elected indirectly by an electoral college for a single 7-year term.
periods.notes: June 1987 Democratic Struggle forced direct elections.

periods.name: Sixth Republic
periods.succession: President directly elected for a single 5-year term. Impeachment by 2/3 of the National Assembly suspends the president; the Constitutional Court decides removal (Roh 2004 reinstated; Park 2017 and Yoon 2025 removed). PM appointed by the president with Assembly consent; acting president in a vacancy; new election within 60 days.
periods.notes: Game: no no-confidence; removal by impeachment + court ruling or end of the single term. A failed self-coup (martial law) is a modeled path (2024).

nations.name: South Vietnam (State of Vietnam / Republic of Vietnam)

periods.name: State of Vietnam (associated state of the French Union)
periods.succession: Former emperor Bao Dai as Chief of State (Quoc truong) under the Elysee Accords (Mar 1949); prime ministers appointed and dismissed by Bao Dai.
periods.notes: Limited sovereignty under France until 1954. After Geneva (Jul 1954) confined to south of the 17th parallel. Bao Dai deposed by Diem's rigged referendum of 23 Oct 1955.

periods.name: First Republic of Vietnam (Ngo Dinh Diem)
periods.succession: Presidential republic (1956 constitution) dominated by the Ngo family and the Can Lao party; no prime minister.
periods.notes: Ended by the ARVN generals' coup of 1-2 Nov 1963 (Diem and Nhu killed) with US acquiescence.

periods.name: Military juntas
periods.succession: Military Revolutionary Council (Duong Van Minh); Nguyen Khanh coup Jan 1964; repeated coups and a civilian interlude (Phan Khac Suu / Tran Van Huong / Phan Huy Quat); National Leadership Committee (Thieu chairman, Ky PM) from Jun 1965.
periods.notes: Game: extreme instability - frequent coup checks.

periods.name: Second Republic of Vietnam (Nguyen Van Thieu)
periods.succession: 1967 constitution: directly elected president (Thieu 1967, unopposed 1971). PM appointed by the president.
periods.notes: Fell to North Vietnam on 30 Apr 1975; Provisional Revolutionary Government nominally ruled the South until reunification (2 Jul 1976).

nations.name: Sweden

periods.name: Kingdom of Sweden (Gustavian absolutism)
periods.succession: Gustav III (assassinated 1792), Gustav IV Adolf (deposed by officers' coup 1809). Not covered in detail (tier 2).
periods.notes: Outside required coverage; generic absolute-monarchy titles apply.

periods.name: Kingdom of Sweden (1809 Instrument of Government, royal government)
periods.succession: Hereditary Bernadotte dynasty (from 1818). Ministers appointed by and responsible to the King; the Riksdag controlled taxation. Union with Norway 1814-1905. Office of Prime Minister (statsminister) from 1876.
periods.notes: Courtyard Crisis 1914: Gustaf V's intervention forced Staaff out - royal dismissal was still possible.

periods.name: Kingdom of Sweden (parliamentary democracy)
periods.succession: Parliamentarism accepted from Edén's government (1917). Under the 1974 Instrument of Government the Speaker nominates the PM and the Riksdag tolerates him unless an absolute majority (175 of 349) votes against (negative parliamentarism); a declaration of no confidence (misstroendeförklaring) by an absolute majority forces the PM or a minister out (Löfven lost one in Jun 2021).
periods.notes: Neutral/non-aligned through both World Wars and the Cold War; joined the EU 1995 and NATO 7 Mar 2024.

nations.name: Ukraine

periods.name: Part of the Russian Empire (Galicia under Austria)
periods.capital: (Kiev was a Russian governorate seat; Lemberg/Lviv in Austrian Galicia)
periods.succession: No Ukrainian state; the Cossack Hetmanate was abolished by 1764 and fully incorporated in 1780s. Not playable; use RUS (and AUT for Galicia).

periods.name: Ukrainian People's Republic / Ukrainian State (Hetmanate) / Directory
periods.capital: Kyiv (frequently lost; government moved to Vinnytsia, Kamianets-Podilskyi)
periods.succession: Central Rada (1917-Apr 1918) overthrown by the German-backed coup of Hetman Pavlo Skoropadsky (Apr-Dec 1918), who was in turn overthrown by the Directory (Dec 1918). Contested by the Bolsheviks, Whites and Poland; the Treaty of Riga (Mar 1921) divided Ukraine between Soviet Russia and Poland. Government-in-exile continued to 1992.
periods.notes: Civil-war state: game should treat as unstable, removal by coup/foreign occupation.

periods.name: Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic
periods.succession: Constituent republic of the USSR from Dec 1922 (founding UN member 1945) but not sovereign: party leaders appointed by Moscow. Not playable separately; use RUS.
periods.notes: 1941-44 under German occupation (Reichskommissariat Ukraine).

periods.name: Ukraine (independence; amended Soviet-era constitution)
periods.succession: Independence declared 24 Aug 1991, confirmed by referendum 1 Dec 1991 (Kravchuk elected president the same day). Early presidential and parliamentary elections in 1994 after a Donbas miners' strike crisis.

periods.name: Ukraine (1996 constitution, presidential-parliamentary)
periods.succession: President directly elected for 5 years (max two consecutive terms) and could dismiss the PM; the Rada could pass no confidence in the cabinet (e.g. Yushchenko cabinet, Apr 2001). The 2004 Orange Revolution forced a re-run of the presidential run-off (Yushchenko defeated Yanukovych).

periods.name: Ukraine (2004 amendments, parliamentary-presidential)
periods.succession: PM nominated by the parliamentary majority coalition and appointed by the Rada; president nominates only the foreign and defence ministers. The Constitutional Court restored the 1996 text in Oct 2010.

periods.name: Ukraine (1996 constitution restored)
periods.succession: Yanukovych fled during the Revolution of Dignity (Euromaidan); on 22 Feb 2014 the Rada voted him 'self-removed' from office (not a constitutional impeachment) and named Turchynov acting president.

periods.name: Ukraine (2004 amendments restored)
periods.succession: President directly elected for 5 years; impeachment needs 2/3 then 3/4 of the Rada plus court opinions (never used). The PM and cabinet are appointed by and responsible to the Rada (no-confidence possible, not within a year of approving the programme); the president nominates the PM (on the coalition's proposal) and the foreign and defence ministers, and appoints/dismisses the SBU head with Rada consent. Under martial law since 24 Feb 2022 elections are suspended, so Zelensky's 2019-24 term continues until elections can be held.
periods.notes: Russia annexed Crimea (2014) and has occupied parts of the east and south since 2014/2022; full-scale war since Feb 2022.

nations.name: Vietnam

periods.name: Nguyen dynasty under French protectorate (Annam, Tonkin) / French Indochina
periods.capital: Hue (imperial court); Hanoi (seat of the Governor-General of Indochina from 1902); Saigon (Cochinchina colony)
periods.succession: Emperors chosen/approved by the French Resident-Superior; Thanh Thai (1907) and Duy Tan (1916) were deposed and exiled by France.
periods.notes: Not sovereign: the French Governor-General of Indochina held real power. The court's Co Mat (Privy Council) ministers were figureheads. Japanese occupation from Sep 1940 (Vichy French administration left in place).

periods.name: Empire of Vietnam (Japanese client state)
periods.succession: After the Japanese coup against the French (9 Mar 1945) Bao Dai proclaimed independence; Tran Trong Kim cabinet.
periods.notes: Ended by the Viet Minh August Revolution; Bao Dai abdicated 25/30 Aug 1945.

periods.name: Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam from 1954)
periods.capital: Hanoi (government in the Viet Bac jungle base Dec 1946 - Oct 1954)
periods.succession: Proclaimed by Ho Chi Minh 2 Sep 1945. Real power with the Indochinese Communist Party / Vietnam Workers' Party (1951) Politburo. Leadership changes by Central Committee plenum or party congress (e.g. Truong Chinh demoted after the 1956 land-reform errors; Le Duan First Secretary from the 3rd Congress, 1960).
periods.notes: First Indochina War 1946-54 (Geneva Accords split the country at the 17th parallel); Vietnam War 1955-75; reunification after the fall of Saigon (30 Apr 1975).

periods.name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam
periods.succession: Communist Party of Vietnam congress every five years elects the Central Committee, which elects the Politburo and General Secretary. The National Assembly then 'elects' the State President, Prime Minister and NA Chairman as nominated by the party ('four pillars'). Since 2023-24 anti-corruption campaign, office-holders are frequently removed by forced resignation (Phuc 2023, Thuong 2024, Hue 2024) - model as party_congress.
periods.notes: Doi Moi reforms from the 6th Congress (Dec 1986). 14th Congress (Jan 2026) re-elected To Lam as General Secretary; in Apr 2026 he was also elected State President, combining the top two posts.

role_notes.paramount_leader: The party General Secretary is the real ruler and the game's player office for the DRV/SRV; State President and PM are senior advisors ('four pillars' collective leadership with the NA Chairman). Removal only via Central Committee/Politburo (party_congress) or death.
role_notes.head_of_state: 1883-1945 the French Governor-General of Indochina (e.g. Paul Doumer 1897-1902, Albert Sarraut 1911-14/1917-19, Jean Decoux 1940-45) held real power; emperors were figureheads. Game: not playable before Sep 1945 (or treat France as owner).
role_notes.head_of_government: No responsible cabinet under the protectorate; the emperor's Co Mat (Privy Council) had no autonomy.
role_notes.interior: DRV Interior Ministry (civil) 1945-; Ministry of Public Security (police and intelligence) from 1953, renamed Ministry of the Interior 1975-1998, then Public Security again. For the game the Public Security minister is the interior/security advisor.
role_notes.intelligence: No separate public intelligence chief: domestic and foreign intelligence (General Department of Security / General Department V) sit within the Ministry of Public Security; military intelligence (General Department II) is under Defence and its chiefs are not public. Game: use the interior (Public Security) holder as intelligence chief.
role_notes.military_chief: Vo Nguyen Giap was Commander-in-Chief of the VPA throughout 1945-1980 and outranked the Chief of the General Staff; for 1946-1975 the game may prefer Giap as military chief.

uncertain: Defence minister / Chief of General Staff handover 1991 vs 1992 (Le Duc Anh -> Doan Khue; Doan Khue -> Dao Dinh Luyen).
Public Security / Interior ministers 1953-1996: years only.
Phan Ke Toai's interior tenure (1947-1963) not cross-checked.

April 2026 government: To Lam (President), Le Minh Hung (PM), Le Hoai Trung (FM), Phan Van Giang (Defence), Ngo Van Tuan (Finance), Luong Tam Quang (Public Security) confirmed by Vietnamese state media and Wikipedia; Chief of General Staff after the 14th Congress not verified.
